In everyday speech they often say something that set him off or a trigger. Saying something was a provocation implies the other person intended to stir things up, so it is a serious accusation.

distinctions.note: Irritation is a mild annoyance felt inside, while provocation is an external act or remark that deliberately provokes a response.
Incitement is the legal term for encouraging others to commit violence; provocation is broader and may not involve any call to action.

examples.everyday: He's usually calm, but a rude comment about his mom was a real provocation for him.
examples.professional: Leadership treated the public comment as a provocation and asked communications to prepare a measured response.
examples.analytical: Whether an offense counts as provocation depends on whether the agent intended to elicit a response or merely caused one.

nuance.analogy: A provocation is like a match struck near a fuse: the spark itself is small, but it is the thing that sets off the explosion.
nuance.etymology: From Latin provocatio, a challenge or appeal, from provocare, to call forth.
common_mistakes: Confusing provocation with provocative; provocation is the act, provocative is the adjective describing it.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying prov-uh-KAY-shun with a short first vowel rather than prah.

provocation.etymology: From Middle English *provocacioun*, from Old French *provocacion*, from Late Latin *provocatio*, from Latin *prōvocō*.

senses.definition: One placed in charge: a head, a chief, particularly: A ruler.
senses.example: The provost of the old city was feared by every merchant who paid tribute.

senses.definition: The minister of the chief Protestant church of a town or region in Germany, the Low Countries, and Scandinavia.
senses.example: After Sunday service, the provost invited the choir to lunch at the parsonage.

senses.definition: A senior deputy, a superintendent, particularly: A viceroy. A governor. A reeve.
senses.example: The provost governed the frontier district on behalf of the king.

senses.definition: A senior deputy administrator; a vice-president of academic affairs.
A title of the archangel Michael.
senses.example: Saint Michael the Archangel is often called the provost of the heavenly host in medieval texts.

senses.definition: An officer of the military police, particularly provost marshal or provost sergeant.
senses.example: The provost arrested two drunken soldiers outside the base's gate on Friday night.

senses.definition: (historical) A dean: the head of a cathedral chapter.
senses.example: The provost presided over the cathedral chapter and managed its finances for the bishop.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A prior: an abbot's second-in-command.
senses.example: The provost stood in for the abbot whenever he traveled to Rome.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A steward or seneschal: a medieval agent given management of a feudal estate or charged with collecting fees.
senses.example: The provost collected rents from the tenants and reported every harvest to the lord.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Any manager or overseer in a medieval or early modern context.
senses.example: As provost of the monastery's granary, Brother Anselm measured every sack of grain.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A constable: a medieval or early modern official charged with arresting, holding, and punishing criminals.
senses.example: The provost led the men through the village to arrest the suspected thief.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) An assistant fencing master.
senses.example: The provost corrected my footwork before I faced the master in the afternoon bout.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A senior university administrator, usually second to the president, who oversees academic programs and faculty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PROH. The 'o' is a long 'oh' sound, and the final 'st' is a clear, short ending, not 'pro-vest'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a professional job title with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American universities, the provost is usually the chief academic officer, often called the 'provost and vice president for academic affairs.' Americans say 'dean' for the head of a single college or school. In everyday talk, people might say 'the provost's office' when discussing university policy.

distinctions.note: A dean leads one college or school within a university, while a provost oversees academic affairs for the whole institution.
A president handles overall leadership, fundraising, and external relations, while a provost focuses mainly on academic programs and faculty.

examples.everyday: I'm going to the provost's office tomorrow to ask about the transfer policy for my son.
examples.professional: The provost approved the budget for the new engineering building after the faculty senate voted.
examples.analytical: The provost's authority over academic standards makes the office central to the university's intellectual identity.

nuance.analogy: A provost is like the chief operating officer of a university's academic life, ensuring that teaching and research run smoothly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English profost, from Medieval Latin praepositus, 'one placed in front' or 'one set over'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'provost' with 'prophet' because of the similar spelling.
Using 'provost' to mean a dean of one college, when it refers to the chief academic officer of the whole university.

provost.etymology: From Middle English, from late Old English *prōfost*, *prāfost*, from Late Latin *prōpositus*, variant of Latin *praepositus* (“[one] placed in command”).

senses.definition: In a psychical or psychic manner.
Mentally.

core.definition: In a way that relates to the mind or soul rather than the body, or in a supernatural mental manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'. Keep the p silent and do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, somewhat literary word, and it can sound unusual or technical in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use psychically in conversation. You may see it in psychology, philosophy, or literary writing about mental or spiritual states. In everyday talk people would more often say mentally, emotionally, or in their head.

distinctions.note: Mentally is the everyday word, while psychically is a more formal or literary way to indicate the soul or psyche.
Emotionally focuses on feelings, while psychically covers the broader mind or soul.

examples.everyday: Honestly, I'm psychically exhausted after that week, even though my body feels fine.
examples.professional: The team lead was physically in the room but psychically checked out, so the decisions stalled.
examples.analytical: The patient was psychically wounded by the trauma, a claim that requires careful definition before it can be tested.

nuance.analogy: Being psychically present is like a radio that is turned on but not tuned in: the signal is there, but the mind is elsewhere.
nuance.etymology: From psychic, from Greek psychikos, meaning of the soul or mind, with the English suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Using psychically as a synonym for psychic when describing paranormal people.
Pronouncing the initial p, which is silent.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the Puritans, or to their doctrines and practice.
senses.example: The historian traced the town's strict Sunday customs back to its puritanical founders in Massachusetts.

senses.definition: Precise in observance of legal or religious requirements; strict; overscrupulous; rigid (often used by way of reproach or contempt).
senses.example: My aunt's puritanical rules forbade any music, cards, or dancing in her house, even on holidays.

senses.definition: One who holds puritanical attitudes.
senses.example: The new board chair is a puritanical who banned coffee from every meeting.

core.definition: Extremely strict about moral behavior, especially about pleasure, dress, or sex, often in a way that others find excessive.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TAN, the third syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced ih. The final syllable is a light kul, not a full ka-lay.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually criticizes someone for being excessively strict or disapproving about morality or pleasure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use puritanical as an insult for people who are overly strict about fun, drinking, sex, or dress. It often appears in news, opinion pieces, and casual complaints about rules. Be careful, because it can offend religious people, so use it for excessive strictness rather than for ordinary faith. A neutral alternative is strict or conservative.

distinctions.note: Strict is neutral and describes following rules closely. Puritanical is critical and suggests an excessive, joyless approach to morality.
Prudish describes someone who is easily shocked by sex or nudity. Puritanical has a broader sense of strict moral disapproval.
Conservative describes a cautious or traditional outlook. Puritanical is more disapproving and suggests harsh moral policing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks any music after nine is too loud, which is a bit puritanical if you ask me.
examples.professional: The manager's puritanical policy on casual Fridays made the team feel watched and resentful.
examples.analytical: Scholars often trace the puritanical tone of some modern moral campaigns to a longer tradition of distrust toward pleasure.

nuance.analogy: A puritanical rule is like a fence built so high that nobody can enjoy the garden behind it.
nuance.etymology: From Puritan, from the English religious group of the 16th and 17th centuries, plus the suffix -ical.
common_mistakes: Using puritanical as a neutral word for religious, when it is usually an insult.
Saying PURE-ih-tan-ih-kal, with the stress on the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: Move a meeting to a later time.

core.definition: To move a scheduled meeting to a later date or time, often because people are unavailable or more preparation is needed.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'the' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant, and 'meeting' has its stress on the first syllable, MEE-ting. Keep the words flowing together in speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical business phrase that is polite when you explain the reason.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, people often say 'Can we push the meeting to Thursday?' or 'Let's push the meeting by an hour'. It sounds natural in email and chat, and it is more casual than 'reschedule'. A good reply is 'Sure, what time works for you?' or 'Sounds good, I'll send a new invite'.

distinctions.note: Reschedule is more formal and neutral, often used in calendar or official notices; push the meeting is more conversational.
Cancel means the meeting will not happen at all; push the meeting means it will happen later.

collocations: push the meeting to next week
push the meeting by an hour

examples.everyday: Hey, my car broke down, so could we push the dinner plans to seven?
examples.professional: Can we push the meeting to Thursday, since the vendor will not send the revised numbers until then?
examples.analytical: Pushing the meeting may appear to be a small logistical choice, but it changes which decisions are made with complete data.

nuance.analogy: Pushing the meeting is like sliding a book on a shelf to a later spot, so it is still there but at a different time.
common_mistakes: Saying 'push the meeting for Friday'; the usual preposition is 'to' or 'until', as in 'push the meeting to Friday'.
Using 'push' for a meeting that is moved earlier; Americans usually say 'move up the meeting' for an earlier time.

conversation.text: Can we push the meeting to three?
They pushed the meeting to next week because the CEO was out.
Let's push the meeting by half an hour so everyone can join.

senses.definition: The act or process of qualifying for a position, achievement etc.
senses.example: Qualification for this organization is extraordinarily difficult.

senses.definition: An ability or attribute that aids someone's chances of qualifying for something; specifically, completed professional training.
senses.example: What are your qualifications for this job?

senses.definition: A clause or condition which qualifies something; a modification, a limitation.
senses.example: I accept your offer, but with the following qualification.

core.definition: A skill, certificate, or requirement that makes a person suitable for a job or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on KAY, the fourth syllable, with secondary stress on the first. The middle vowels are reduced, and the ending -tion sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means credentials, and neutral or cautious when it means a limiting condition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use qualification most often for credentials, such as 'the minimum qualifications for the job' or 'a degree is a qualification.' In speech, people usually say 'requirements' or 'experience' for the same idea. In legal or contract language, a qualification can be a condition or limitation, so it sounds formal.

distinctions.note: A credential is a document proving a skill; a qualification is broader and can include experience or training.
A requirement is something mandatory; a qualification is what makes you eligible, and it can be preferred rather than required.

examples.everyday: My neighbor has the qualifications to teach piano, since she has a music degree and fifteen years of experience.
examples.professional: The job posting lists a bachelor's degree as a minimum qualification, but relevant work experience is also valued.
examples.analytical: Her claim holds without qualification, though the argument would be stronger if she specified the conditions under which the results apply.

nuance.analogy: A qualification is like a ticket to enter a room: it shows you have met the entry requirements.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin qualificatio, from qualificare 'to qualify', from Latin qualis 'of what kind' and facere 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Using qualification for the verb 'qualify', as in 'he qualification for the job'.
Confusing the sense of credentials with the sense of a limiting condition in formal writing.

qualification.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *qualification* in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin *quālificātiō*.

senses.definition: Capable of being quantified.
senses.example: The team's goal was to make customer satisfaction quantifiable through a monthly survey score.

senses.definition: Something that can be quantified; a measurable.
senses.example: Her manager insisted that every project be reported in quantifiables, such as hours saved and dollars earned.

core.definition: Able to be measured or expressed as a number or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KWAHN. The -tuh- and -uh- syllables are reduced to schwa, and the -ble ending is a quick, unstressed buhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes whether something can be turned into a number.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quantifiable often in business, science and policy talk, as in 'quantifiable results'. It is rarely needed in casual talk, where 'measurable' or 'you can count it' works. Its noun use is uncommon.

distinctions.note: Measurable is broader and can mean large enough to notice; quantifiable specifically means it can be turned into a number.
Quantitative describes methods or data based on numbers; quantifiable describes whether something can be expressed in numbers at all.

examples.everyday: The cost savings aren't really quantifiable, but everyone feels less stressed since we switched.
examples.professional: Leadership wants quantifiable results before they approve the second phase.
examples.analytical: Not every human good is quantifiable, which is why ethics cannot be reduced to accounting.

nuance.analogy: Like weighing flour on a scale: some things come with a number on them.
nuance.etymology: Built from quantity and the suffix -able; quantity comes from Latin quantitas, 'how much'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; say KWAHN-tuh-fy-uh-buhl.
Using quantifiable for anything large; it means can be turned into a number.

senses.definition: A trembling shake.
senses.example: The candle flame gave a quaver in the draft from the open door.

senses.definition: A trembling of the voice, as in speaking or singing.
senses.example: Her voice had a quaver when she spoke about her late father.

senses.definition: An eighth note, drawn as a crotchet (quarter note) with a tail.
senses.example: In 4/4 time, a quaver receives half a beat, so two of them fill one beat.

senses.definition: To shake in a trembling manner.
To use the voice in a trembling manner, as in speaking or singing.
To utter quaveringly.
senses.example: The old man quavered his reply, afraid the customs officer would refuse him entry.

core.definition: To shake or tremble, especially the voice, while speaking or singing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, 'KWAY'. The final syllable is a reduced American 'r' sound, so it sounds like 'vur' rather than 'vah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, implying nervousness, fear or emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'quaver' mainly for a voice that trembles from emotion, nervousness or age, as in 'Her voice quavered during the toast.' As a noun, it is also used in music for an eighth note. In everyday talk, 'shake' or 'tremble' is more common, so 'quaver' sounds a bit literary.

distinctions.note: 'Tremble' is common for any shaking; 'quaver' focuses on the voice or a sound that wavers.
'Shake' can describe the whole body; 'quaver' is usually limited to voice or a thin, unsteady sound.
'Waver' means to hesitate or become unsteady in decisions or strength; 'quaver' refers to a physical trembling of a sound.

examples.everyday: When the neighbor called about the noise, his voice quavered a little, and I could tell he was nervous.
examples.professional: During the meeting, Dan's voice quavered when he admitted the model had failed in production.
examples.analytical: The poet's voice quavers between confidence and doubt, and the rhythm mirrors that instability.

nuance.analogy: A quaver is like a flame in a draft: it flickers and shakes but stays lit.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'quaveren', likely related to Old English 'cwafian' (to tremble).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'kwav-er' with a short 'a' like 'quaver' in 'waver'; it has a long 'ay' sound.
Using 'quaver' for general shaking of objects, where 'shake' or 'tremble' fits better.

quaver.etymology: From Middle English *quaveren*, frequentative form of *quaven*, *cwavien* (“to tremble”), equivalent to *quave* + *er*.

senses.definition: A worded or expressed sentence, phrase, or only a word on its own, which asks for information, a reply, or a response; an interrogative.
senses.example: What is your question?

senses.definition: A subject or topic for consideration or investigation.
senses.example: The question of seniority will be discussed at the meeting.

senses.definition: A doubt or challenge about the truth, accuracy, or validity of a matter.
senses.example: His claim to the property has come under question.

senses.definition: A proposal to a meeting as a topic for deliberation.
senses.example: I move that the question be put to a vote.

senses.definition: To ask questions of; to interrogate; to ask for information.
senses.example: The detectives questioned every witness who had been near the warehouse that night.

senses.definition: To raise doubts about; have doubts about.
senses.example: Several economists began to question the accuracy of the unemployment figures after the revision.

senses.definition: To ask a question or questions; inquire or seek to know; examine.
senses.example: My theology professor taught us to question every assumption we brought into class.

core.definition: A sentence, phrase, or word that asks for information, a reply, or a response; a request for an answer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The '-tion' ending is pronounced 'chuhn,' not 'shun' or 'tee-on,' and the middle 'ti' sounds like 'ch.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Asking a question is normal and polite in nearly all American contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use question constantly in everyday talk to ask for information politely. 'Quick question' is a common, friendly opener. In a meeting, you can say 'Can I ask a question?' or 'I have a question about this slide.' In a more formal setting, 'May I ask a question?' is appropriate.

distinctions.note: Inquiry is more formal and suggests a systematic investigation, while a question is a single request for information.
Query is more technical and common in databases and software, where it means a formal request for data.
Issue means a problem or a topic under discussion, while question can also mean a doubt about something.

examples.everyday: Quick question: do you know if the hardware store is still open on Sundays?
examples.professional: Before we approve the budget, I have one question about the cloud costs for the staging environment.
examples.analytical: The central question of the essay is whether moral knowledge can be reached without any form of revelation.

nuance.analogy: A question is a key that opens a door to an answer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quaestio, a seeking or inquiry, from quaerere, to seek.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a question' instead of 'ask a question.'
Mispronouncing the ending as 'KWES-tee-on' with a separate 'tee' and 'on' syllable.

question.etymology: From Middle English *questioun*, from Anglo-Norman *questiun*, from Old French *question*, from Latin *quaestiōnem*, accusative of *quaestiō* (“a seeking, investigation, inquiry, question”), from *quaerere* (“to seek, ask, inquire”), of uncertain origin,…

senses.definition: Mentally keen and alert.
senses.example: She was far too quick-witted to miss the implications of what he was saying.

core.definition: Able to think and respond quickly and cleverly, especially in conversation or under pressure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WIT, the second element. The -ted ending is flapped to a soft 'd' sound, so it's 'WIT-id' rather than 'wit-ted'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises fast, clever thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quick-witted to praise someone with a fast comeback or who can answer hard questions on the spot, often in conversation, interviews or teaching. It usually describes a person, though 'a quick-witted reply' is also natural. In a formal evaluation you might say 'thinks on her feet'. A natural reply to a compliment is 'Thanks, I got lucky'.

distinctions.note: Witty means funny in a clever way with words; quick-witted means fast in thinking, which can be serious or practical.
Clever is broad and can describe skill or cunning; quick-witted stresses speed of response.

examples.everyday: My sister is so quick-witted that she always has a comeback for my jokes.
examples.professional: The product lead was quick-witted in the review, answering every hard question on the spot.
examples.analytical: The novel's detective is quick-witted rather than systematic, so she solves crimes through intuition and nerve.

nuance.analogy: Like a goalkeeper who reacts to a shot before the striker finishes the kick.
nuance.etymology: Quick from Old English cwic, 'alive'; wit from Old English witt, 'mind, intelligence'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'quick witted' before a noun without the hyphen.
Confusing it with witty, which emphasizes humor rather than speed of thought.

senses.definition: In a manner that is radiant; glowingly.
senses.example: She smiled radiantly at the crowd as the newlyweds walked down the aisle.

core.definition: In a way that shows bright, happy energy, often in a very visible way such as glowing with joy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, RAY. Say it as three quick syllables, with the second and third unstressed, and do not add an extra vowel between the d and the -ent.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's visible happiness, confidence or beauty, though it can sound a bit dramatic in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use radiantly most often to describe someone's smile, face or confidence, usually in writing, speeches or warm descriptions. In everyday speech people more often say 'she was glowing' or 'she looked so happy.' It can sound slightly formal or enthusiastic, so it fits best with a compliment or a memorable moment.

distinctions.note: Brightly describes light or color, while radiantly describes a person's visible happiness, beauty or confidence.
Happily describes a general state of mind, while radiantly suggests a bright, shining quality that others can see.

examples.everyday: She smiled radiantly when she saw her daughter walk across the stage at graduation.
examples.professional: The new team lead presented the quarterly numbers and looked radiantly confident in front of the executives.
examples.analytical: The painting shows the Virgin Mary standing radiantly in gold light, which makes her the visual center of the scene.

nuance.analogy: A radiant face is like a lamp turned up: the happiness inside is visible from across the room.
nuance.etymology: From radiant, from Latin radiare, to shine or emit rays.
common_mistakes: Using 'radiantly' for physical light alone; for light, 'brightly' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as one long vowel: say RAY-dee-ent-lee.

senses.definition: Any of various radical social or political movements that aim at fundamental change in the structure of society.

core.definition: Support for sweeping political or social change that seeks to alter the basic structure of society.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllables so the word has a quick, even rhythm ending in 'ism'. The final syllable is a soft 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can describe principled reform or extremist views, depending on who uses it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use radicalism in political history, news, and academic discussion, often to describe movements of the 1960s or current debates. It can sound like criticism when used by people who disagree with the movement. In everyday talk, people usually say 'extreme views' or 'activism'.

distinctions.note: Radicalism describes the belief in fundamental change, while extremism describes the use of extreme methods or views that are often rejected by mainstream society.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still talks about the student radicalism of his college days.
examples.professional: The policy team debated whether our proposal was pragmatic or simply radicalism dressed in business language.
examples.analytical: Historians often separate reformist liberalism from the deeper radicalism that demanded the restructuring of property and power.

nuance.analogy: Radicalism is like replacing the foundation of a house rather than repainting the walls.
nuance.etymology: From radical, from Late Latin radicalis, 'of roots', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'cat' instead of 'RAD'; the first vowel is short but clear.
Using radicalism as a neutral synonym for activism; it implies deeper or more sweeping change.

senses.definition: (archaic) Immoral; dissolute.
senses.label: archaic

senses.definition: (archaic) A lewd or wanton person; a debauchee; a rake.
senses.example: Don't trust that rakehell, Margaret; he has ruined three honest families already.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Immoral and dissolute; living a wild, debauched life, as in older novels or formal writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable strongly and give the second syllable a lighter secondary stress. The final 'hell' is a simple 'hel' sound, not 'hell' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes serious moral disorder and is rarely used in modern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'rakehell' in daily life. It appears mainly in older novels, historical writing, or deliberately formal prose. In modern English, say 'dissolute' or 'debauched' in writing, or 'wild' and 'reckless' in speech.

distinctions.note: 'Rake' is the common word for a dissolute man, while 'rakehell' is an older, more emphatic adjective or noun with a stronger flavor of immorality.
A libertine rejects moral restraint in sexual matters, while a rakehell is more broadly dissolute and wild in conduct.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said her cousin had a rakehell youth, but he settled down after he married.
examples.professional: The novel's rakehell hero serves as a foil for the sober, principled narrator.
examples.analytical: Richardson's rakehell seducer embodies the moral danger the novel warns against, making his fall the center of the moral argument.

nuance.analogy: A rakehell is like a ship with no steering, drifting wherever its appetites take it.
nuance.etymology: From rake (a dissolute man) and hell, from the 17th-century sense of a wild, reckless person.
common_mistakes: Using 'rakehell' in casual speech, where it sounds dated and theatrical.
Confusing 'rakehell' with 'rake' as a verb or tool.

rakehell.etymology: From to rake hell (“to search through hell thoroughly”), in the sense of a person so evil or immoral that they cannot be found in hell even after an extensive search: see *rake* (“to search through”).

senses.definition: In a rampant manner.

core.definition: In a widespread, uncontrolled way, spreading or growing without any check, usually for harmful things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAM. Say the -ant- as a weak 'unt' and keep the -ly ending as 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests something spreading out of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rampantly in news writing, analysis and formal discussion of problems such as crime, inflation or disease. Casual speakers would more often say 'everywhere' or 'out of control'. It usually comes before the verb or adjective it modifies.

distinctions.note: Widely is a neutral word for something being common or known, while rampantly suggests an uncontrolled, harmful spread.
Extensively means thoroughly or over a large area, while rampantly stresses that growth is unchecked.
Commonly describes frequency and is neutral, while rampantly describes a dangerous or unrestrained spread.

examples.everyday: Mold was growing rampantly in the basement after the flood, so we called a cleaning crew right away.
examples.professional: Shadow IT has spread rampantly across the company, so the security team now has to track unapproved tools.
examples.analytical: If an institution is rampantly corrupt, reform requires more than replacing a few individuals, because the habits are built into its structure.

nuance.analogy: Like crabgrass taking over a lawn: unchecked, it spreads into every patch until the whole yard is covered.
nuance.etymology: From rampant (from Old French ramper 'to crawl or climb') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing it awkwardly, such as 'spread rampantly is' instead of 'is spreading rampantly'.
Using it for positive growth; it almost always describes something harmful.
Confusing it with rampantly as a noun form; the noun is rampancy.

senses.definition: The property of being capable of being read; legibility.
The property of being easy or engaging to read.
senses.example: The book had a clever plot, but lacked readability.

core.definition: How easy a text is to read and understand, or the quality of being clear and legible.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'bil,' and the '-ability' ending is pronounced 'uh-BIL-uh-tee.' Do not stress the first syllable or pronounce 'ability' as 'a-BEE-li-ty.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it is a desirable quality in writing and design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'readability' in technical writing, software design, education, and marketing. It can refer to text, code, or interfaces, and in code reviews it often means that code is clear to other developers. In casual speech people say 'easy to read' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Legibility' concerns how clearly letters or characters can be distinguished; 'readability' concerns how easily a whole text is understood.
'Clarity' is a broader quality of meaning; 'readability' focuses on ease of reading the text itself.

examples.everyday: This article has great readability, so I finished it in one sitting.
examples.professional: During code review, we flagged several functions for poor readability before merging the pull request.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of language have long debated whether a text's readability reflects its clarity of thought or merely its surface simplicity.

nuance.analogy: Readability is like a well-lit path through a forest: the destination is easy to follow because the route is clear.
nuance.etymology: From 'readable' (from 'read,' Old English 'rǣdan') plus the suffix '-ability,' from Latin '-abilis.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, as in 'REE-da-bil-i-ty.'
Confusing it with 'readability' as a synonym for 'literacy,' which is a different concept.

senses.definition: Any type of spectacles intended chiefly to deal with the effects of presbyopia by magnifying details such as fine text.
senses.example: I bought reading glasses at the pharmacy so I could see the small print on menus.

core.definition: Eyeglasses with magnifying lenses worn to help you see small print and close-up objects, typically because of presbyopia.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on GLASS, the second word, while reading has only a light secondary stress. The final -es is a reduced /əz/, so say GLASS-uhz, not GLASS-ez, and the ea in reading is a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Some people feel reading glasses signal getting older, so they may joke about them, but the phrase itself is not negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say reading glasses all the time, and they usually buy them at drugstores like CVS or Walgreens in a section of ready-made magnifiers. In casual talk, people often shorten it to readers, as in 'Have you seen my readers?' Glasses are a pair, so say 'a pair of reading glasses' or 'my reading glasses,' not 'a reading glass.'

distinctions.note: Bifocals have two correction zones in one lens, usually for distance and near vision, while reading glasses correct only near vision.
Progressive lenses change gradually from distance to near power with no visible line, whereas reading glasses have one fixed near power.

examples.everyday: I can't read the menu without my reading glasses, so can you read it to me?
examples.professional: Let me grab my reading glasses so I can check these figures in the spreadsheet.
examples.analytical: Reading glasses correct only presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focus, so they cannot address the astigmatism or myopia that a full eye exam might reveal.

nuance.analogy: They are like a magnifying glass you wear on your face: the lenses do the close-up work your eyes can no longer do alone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English rǣdan ('to read, interpret') and glæs ('glass'); the name reflects their use for reading.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a reading glass' for one pair; use 'a pair of reading glasses'.
Stressing the -es ending as a full /ɛz/ syllable instead of a reduced /əz/.

senses.definition: A second or subsequent admission.
senses.example: After her readmission to the hospital, the nurses adjusted her medication schedule.

core.definition: Being admitted again to a hospital, school, program, or other institution after leaving or being discharged.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MISH, the syllable of admission, while re- takes a light secondary stress. The final -sion is pronounced 'shun,' and the middle vowel is short, as in 'bad'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts, but negative in healthcare, where a readmission can signal poor discharge planning or care.
nuance.usage_note: In American healthcare, hospital readmission is a major quality measure, and Medicare penalizes hospitals with high 30-day readmission rates. In everyday talk, people usually say 'he had to go back in' or 'he was readmitted.' Colleges also use the term for students who withdrew and now need to apply to return.

distinctions.note: A return visit or follow-up appointment does not mean being formally admitted again as an inpatient, while readmission does.
Reinstatement restores someone to a job, membership, or position they lost, while readmission lets someone back into an institution they left or were discharged from.
Re-entry means physically coming back into a place, such as a country or a building, whereas readmission is formal permission to be admitted again.

examples.everyday: My dad's blood pressure spiked two days after he went home, so he ended up with a readmission.
examples.professional: Our quality team flagged a 30-day readmission rate above the regional average, so we're reviewing discharge planning.
examples.analytical: Readmission can reflect either premature discharge or the natural course of chronic illness, so raw rates alone are a poor measure of hospital quality.

nuance.analogy: Like a patient walking back through the same door after being sent home, a readmission asks whether the first exit was truly ready.
nuance.etymology: From Latin re- ('again') plus admission, from Latin admittere ('to let in, send to').
common_mistakes: Using 'readmission' for simply returning to a place, such as a gym; say 'I went back' or 'I rejoined'.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'RE-admission'; the main stress falls on MISH.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being reciprocal, e.g. of a relationship between people.
senses.example: In a friendship, reciprocity occurs where the contribution of each party meets the expectations of the other party.

senses.definition: A reciprocal relationship.
A relation of mutual dependence or action or influence.
senses.example: Our friendship rests on a deep reciprocity, with each of us always willing to help the other.

senses.definition: A reciprocal construction involves two noun phrases where each of the participants occupies both the role of agent and patient with respect to the other. see: Wikipedia:Reciprocal pronoun.
senses.example: In linguistics class, we analyzed how reciprocity appears in sentences like 'the twins hugged each other.'

senses.definition: The responses of individuals to the actions of others.
senses.example: Researchers observed strong reciprocity among the chimpanzees, which shared food with those who had groomed them.

senses.definition: The mutual exchange of rights, privileges or obligations between nations. see: Wikipedia:Reciprocity (international relations).
senses.example: Under the treaty, both nations committed to reciprocity, granting each other equal access to their markets.

core.definition: A relationship in which two people or groups give and receive benefits, favors, or actions in equal measure.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on PRAH, the third syllable from the start, with a secondary stress on the first syllable. Americans pronounce the 'ci' as 'sih' in the middle, and the final '-ty' is a short 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals fairness and balance, and it can also describe obligation in trade or diplomacy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reciprocity mostly in academic, legal, diplomatic, and business settings, such as trade agreements or discussions of fairness. In casual conversation they would say 'it goes both ways' or 'we help each other out'. It is rarely used for small everyday favors.

distinctions.note: Mutuality is a more emotional or relational term for shared feeling, while reciprocity stresses an exchange of benefits or actions.
Equality describes the same status or amount, whereas reciprocity describes a back-and-forth exchange that need not be equal in size.

examples.everyday: Our friendship works well because there's real reciprocity; we both help each other out.
examples.professional: The contract is only fair if there is reciprocity, so both teams must share their data and their timelines.
examples.analytical: Many moral theories treat reciprocity as the foundation of justice, since each party's obligations depend on the other's.

nuance.analogy: Like a seesaw: when one side goes up, the other side goes down, and both sides keep the balance together.
nuance.etymology: From reciprocal, from Latin reciprocus, 'moving back and forth'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'see' instead of a reduced 'sih'.
Confusing reciprocity with reciprocation: reciprocity is the relationship, reciprocation is the act of returning something.

senses.definition: Notable; distinguished; honored.
senses.example: She is a recognized expert in Reformation theology, cited by scholars worldwide.

core.definition: Widely accepted or respected as important or authoritative by experts or the public.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ed is pronounced as a d sound, not a separate syllable, because it follows the voiced z sound. Keep the g before n, as in recognize.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals credibility and reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'recognized' before nouns like expert, authority or leader, as in 'a nationally recognized expert.' It is a neutral, polished word for everyday professional talk and formal writing. Do not use it to mean that a face is easy to recognize; use 'recognizable' for that.

distinctions.note: Famous means widely known, sometimes for reasons unrelated to skill; recognized means acknowledged for quality or authority.
Renowned is a stronger, more literary word for a great reputation; recognized is more neutral and common in professional settings.
Accredited refers to an official approval by a body; recognized may be informal public or professional acknowledgment.

examples.everyday: My sister is a recognized expert on sourdough, so I asked her for advice.
examples.professional: The team hired a recognized authority on causal inference to review the model.
examples.analytical: The findings carried weight because they were published in a recognized journal with rigorous peer review.

nuance.analogy: A recognized name is like a brand on a product that people trust before they open it.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of recognize, from Latin recognoscere 'to know again'.
common_mistakes: Using 'recognized' to mean 'recognizable', as in 'a recognized face' for 'a recognizable face'
Forgetting the final d sound, saying REK-uh-gnize-ed

senses.definition: The act of regaling.
senses.example: The regalement of the guests with lavish dinners and fine wine lasted well into the night.

core.definition: The act of entertaining someone lavishly, often with food, drink, music, or stories.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAYL, the second syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa followed by t, so it sounds like 'ment' with a very light vowel, not 'mint'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting pleasant, generous entertainment; can sound old-fashioned or ironic in modern use.
nuance.usage_note: 'Regalement' is rare in American speech and writing; Americans more often say 'entertainment,' 'treat,' or simply 'a feast.' You will meet it mostly in older literature or formal essays. If you use it, it may sound slightly archaic, so a plain word is usually better in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Entertainment' is everyday and general, while 'regalement' suggests a lavish, almost royal feast of food or stories.
'Regale' is the verb: to entertain someone with stories or a feast, whereas 'regalement' is the noun for that act.

examples.professional: The keynote was a regalement of past product wins rather than a plan for next year.
examples.analytical: Such regalement of the senses sits uneasily beside the sermon's call to self-denial.

nuance.analogy: Think of a royal banquet where everything is served generously to honor the guests.
nuance.etymology: From regale (from French régaler) plus -ment.
common_mistakes: Using 'regalement' in everyday conversation where 'entertainment' or 'treat' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'regalia,' which refers to ceremonial symbols of royalty, not to entertaining.

senses.definition: In a relative manner; with reference to environment or competition; contextually or comparatively.
senses.example: The new hybrid car is relatively quiet, though the tires still hum on highways.

senses.definition: Somewhat; fairly.

core.definition: To a moderate degree, or in comparison with something else; fairly or somewhat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REL. In casual speech the middle t often softens into a quick flap, and the final -ly is a clear 'lee.' Don't add an extra syllable after 'tiv.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It softens a statement and is used to hedge or compare.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'relatively' as a hedge, as in 'relatively easy' or 'relatively quiet,' to avoid sounding too absolute. 'Relatively speaking' is a common casual phrase meaning 'compared to other things.' A natural reply to 'Was the drive long?' is 'Relatively short, maybe twenty minutes.'

distinctions.note: Fairly describes a degree directly, as in 'fairly good.' Relatively adds a comparison, as in 'relatively good for this price.'
Comparatively means the same thing and is more formal. Relatively is the everyday choice in American speech.
Quite is stronger and often means 'very.' Relatively is weaker and points to a comparison.

examples.everyday: The hotel was relatively cheap for a place two blocks from the beach.
examples.professional: The new onboarding flow is relatively simple, so we should see fewer support tickets next month.
examples.analytical: The variance is relatively stable across samples, which suggests the estimator is robust to small changes in the data.

nuance.analogy: Relatively is like a ruler held next to another object: it tells you how big something is only by comparison.
nuance.etymology: From relative, from Late Latin relativus, plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'relatively' without a comparison, as in 'The movie was relatively' with nothing after it.
Confusing 'relatively' with 'relevantly,' which means 'in a way that connects to the issue.'
Putting the stress on the second syllable; the stress falls on REL.

senses.definition: In a relentless manner.
In a manner unrelenting or unyielding in severity; unrelentingly.
senses.example: The coach pushed the team relentlessly through every drill in the brutal heat.

senses.definition: In a steady and persistent manner; unceasingly.
senses.example: She followed up with the landlord relentlessly until the repairs were finished.

core.definition: In a continuous way that does not stop or ease up, often in a harsh or determined manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on LENT, and the -ly ending is a light, short ee sound. Keep the first syllable reduced and say the nt cluster quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use relentlessly in news, business and everyday talk to describe steady, nonstop action, such as 'they promoted it relentlessly' or 'the rain fell relentlessly.' It can be positive for determined effort or negative for harsh pressure. It is rarely used in very casual speech.

distinctions.note: Constantly is neutral and very common; relentlessly adds a sense of pressure, determination or harshness.
Unceasingly is more literary and formal; relentlessly is more common in ordinary American English.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog barks relentlessly every time the mail comes, and it drives me crazy.
examples.professional: The product team worked relentlessly to fix the login bug before the holiday launch.
examples.analytical: The author pursues the question relentlessly, refusing every easy answer the tradition has offered.

nuance.analogy: Like a drumbeat that never pauses; the rhythm keeps going whether anyone notices it or not.
nuance.etymology: From relentless, from relent (from Latin lentare 'to bend') with the suffixes -less and -ly.
common_mistakes: Using relentlessly as an adjective; say 'a relentless pace', not 'a relentlessly pace'.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ree' instead of a reduced 'rih'.

senses.definition: In a remarkable manner.
senses.example: He performed the piece remarkably, offering novel interpretations to its nearly cliched passages.

senses.definition: To a noteworthy extent.
senses.example: That dog is remarkably fierce.

senses.definition: Used to draw special attention to a proposition.
senses.example: Remarkably, three State assembly elections were decided by a total of fewer than one hundred votes.

core.definition: In a way that is surprisingly good, unusual, or striking; to a notable degree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAR, and the final '-ably' is pronounced 'uh-blee,' with the middle schwa nearly silent in fast speech. Do not pronounce the 'a' as a long 'ay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It often introduces a surprising fact, and it can soften a statement, as in 'remarkably, nobody got hurt.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'remarkably' often as a sentence adverb at the beginning of a sentence to signal surprise, as in 'Remarkably, the flight was on time.' In everyday speech it is common and not stiff. You can reply with 'Right?' or 'I know,' which show agreement.

distinctions.note: 'Surprisingly' emphasizes the speaker's unexpected reaction, while 'remarkably' emphasizes that the thing itself is striking or noteworthy.
'Especially' ranks one item above others; 'remarkably' highlights an unusual degree or result.

examples.everyday: Remarkably, the pizza showed up before we even finished ordering.
examples.professional: Remarkably, the model's error rate dropped by half after just one retraining cycle.
examples.analytical: Remarkably, Hume's skepticism leaves ordinary causal talk intact while denying its rational foundation.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden clear sky after a week of rain, 'remarkably' marks a result that breaks the usual pattern.
nuance.etymology: From 'remarkable' plus the adverb suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'rih-mar-KAY-bly'; the stress belongs on the first syllable of 'REMARK' within the word's root, as in rih-MAR-kuh-blee.
Using 'remarkably' to mean 'remarkable' in the sense of a noun, as in 'it was a remarkably day.' Use it before adjectives or verbs, not as a substitute for them.

senses.definition: Earnest protest or objection, disapproving pleading, or an act thereof.
senses.example: Despite her earnest remonstration, the board voted to close the community library.

core.definition: A forceful, formal protest or objection to something considered wrong or unfair.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'stray' in the middle. The first syllables are weak and quick, and the final '-tion' sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It describes a serious objection, often one that reflects disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'protest', 'objection', or 'complaint'. 'Remonstration' sounds formal and is used in writing, speeches, or historical accounts. 'Remonstrance' is an equally acceptable form and is slightly more common in American writing.

distinctions.note: Protest is the everyday word for any public or formal objection, while remonstration stresses a reasoned, earnest plea against something.
A complaint is usually casual or routine, while a remonstration is more serious and formal.

examples.everyday: When the neighbors kept parking in front of our driveway, we made a polite but firm remonstration.
examples.professional: The team made a formal remonstration to management about the unrealistic deadline.
examples.analytical: The essay opens with a remonstration against the claim that moral progress is merely a matter of custom.

nuance.analogy: A remonstration is like a sincere 'hey, that's not right' spoken with careful reasons.
nuance.etymology: From Latin remonstrare 'to point out, show', from re- 'back' plus monstrare 'to show'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'remonstration' with 'demonstration', which means a public display or a proof.
Using it in casual conversation, where 'complaint' or 'objection' sounds more natural.
Mispronouncing the stress by placing it on the first syllable.

remonstration.etymology: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin *remōnstrātiō*.

senses.definition: Able to be repeated.
That gives the same results when repeated.
senses.example: A good experiment must be repeatable, so other labs can confirm the results independently.

core.definition: Able to be done, made, or produced again, often with the same result each time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEET, and the ending -able is a reduced syllable pronounced uh-bul, not 'ay-bul' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive in technical and business contexts, where it means reliable and consistent. In casual speech, 'not repeatable' can be a polite euphemism for something rude or obscene.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use repeatable in work settings to praise a process that gives the same result each time, such as a repeatable recipe or deployment. In humor, people say a story is 'not repeatable' to mean it is too rude to tell in public. The word is common in technical writing but would sound stiff if used to describe a casual, one-time event.

distinctions.note: Repeated describes something that already happened several times; repeatable describes whether something can be done again with the same result.
Reproducible is the stronger scientific term, meaning independent people can get the same result; repeatable usually refers to the same person or setup doing it again.
Recurring describes something that happens again without deliberate action; repeatable describes something that can be done again on purpose.

examples.everyday: That pasta recipe is easy to follow and comes out the same every time, so it's really repeatable.
examples.professional: We need a repeatable deployment process so every release goes through the same steps and gets the same checks.
examples.analytical: A claim counts as scientific evidence only if the experiment supporting it is repeatable under clearly stated conditions.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe card that produces the same cake each time you follow it exactly.
nuance.etymology: From repeat plus -able, from Latin repetere 'to seek again' and -abilis 'able to be'.
common_mistakes: Giving the ending -able a long vowel as 'ay-bul'; it is a reduced uh-bul.
Using repeatable for a one-time event, which by definition cannot be repeated on purpose.

core.definition: A Hebrew name borne by several men in the Old Testament, most notably a leader who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, EYE, which is the Hebrew-derived '-iah' ending pronounced as 'eye' plus a light 'uh'. Americans often shorten the middle syllable, so keep it clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a proper name used in religious and academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name mainly in Bible study, Old Testament commentaries, or lists of names in Chronicles and Nehemiah. It is not used in everyday conversation. In a Bible class, you might say 'Rephaiah son of Hur appears in Nehemiah 3:9.'
word_family: Rephaim (proper noun, a related name for an ancient people)

distinctions.note: Rephaiah is a personal name of individual men; Rephaim is the name of an ancient people of giant stature.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading Nehemiah this month, and we keep getting stuck on all those names like Rephaiah.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I'm grouping the wall-builders in Nehemiah 3 so students can see who repaired which section.
examples.analytical: The chronicler's genealogy names Rephaiah among the descendants of David's line, which signals the family's continuing place in the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a building's cornerstone, Rephaiah marks one worker among many who helped restore Jerusalem.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew name Rephayah, 'Yahweh has healed' (from rapha, 'to heal', with the divine name shortened).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'REF-ay-eye-uh' with the stress on the first syllable.
Confusing Rephaiah, a man's name, with Rephaim, the name of an ancient people.
nuance.biblical_note: Several men named Rephaiah appear in the Old Testament. Nehemiah 3:9 says Rephaiah son of Hur was ruler of half the district of Jerusalem and helped repair the wall. 1 Chronicles 3:21 lists a Rephaiah among the descendants of Zerubbabel's line, and 1 Chronicles 4:42 and 7:2 mention other men with the name. The name means 'Yahweh has healed.'

senses.definition: A company agent who visits potential purchasers; a salesman.
senses.example: The pharmaceutical representative visited our clinic every Tuesday to pitch new products.

senses.definition: A delegate.
senses.example: She served four terms as representative of her local at the national union convention.

senses.definition: Someone who represents others as a member of a legislative or governing body.
senses.example: She served four terms as representative of her local at the national union convention.

senses.definition: One who speaks for or acts on behalf of another in a particular (especially official) capacity.
senses.example: I will send a representative to work out the details of the contract.

senses.definition: An heir.
senses.example: As the sole representative of the estate, she inherited the house and its debts.

senses.definition: Specifically, a member of the United States House of Representatives.
senses.example: All representatives face re-election every two years.

senses.definition: Something standing for something else.
senses.example: In the painting, the lamb is a representative of innocence and sacrifice.

senses.definition: Something representing or standing for another; a symbol, an embodiment.
senses.example: For many voters, the senator was a representative of the town's stubborn independence.

senses.definition: A member of a particular class.
senses.example: Each county sent one representative to the regional planning committee meeting.

senses.definition: Something (especially a living organism) regarded as typical of its class; a type.
senses.example: The house finch is a representative of the songbirds common in our backyard.

senses.definition: A consistent choice of element from an equivalence class, used to identify it.
senses.example: In a quotient group, each coset is identified by a chosen representative element.

senses.definition: A substitute or analogue.
senses.example: Almond milk is a common representative of dairy in our household's recipes.

senses.definition: Typical; having the same properties or interest as a larger group.
senses.example: The survey sample was representative of the city's diverse population.

senses.definition: Representing, showing a likeness.
senses.example: Are you sure this paper is representative of your child's writing?

core.definition: A person who speaks, sells or handles requests for a company or organization on its behalf, often by phone or in person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZEN, and the ending -ative reduces to a short tiv. The middle ta is often nearly silent in fast speech, so the word sounds like three main syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a plain job title, though sales contexts can feel slightly pushy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often shorten it to 'rep' in casual speech, as in 'Let me talk to a rep.' 'Sales rep' and 'customer service rep' are everyday terms. As an adjective, representative is more formal, and the noun for an elected lawmaker, as in a U.S. House representative, is political.

distinctions.note: An agent can be someone with authority to act for another person; a rep is more common for a company employee who handles sales or service.
A delegate is chosen to attend a meeting or convention; a representative is usually an elected lawmaker or a company's official spokesperson.

examples.everyday: I was on hold for an hour, so I finally asked to speak to a representative.
examples.professional: Please have the sales representative send the revised contract to our procurement team by Friday.
examples.analytical: A sample is representative only if its members resemble the population on the variables that matter to the question.

nuance.analogy: Like a company's spokesperson on a phone line: the voice that stands in for the whole firm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin repraesentare 'to present again, make present'.
common_mistakes: Using it for an elected official in casual speech; most Americans say 'congressman' or 'legislator' instead.
Confusing the adjective meaning 'typical' with the noun meaning 'person who acts for others'.

representative.etymology: From Middle English *representative*, from Middle French *representatif* and its etymon Medieval Latin *repraesentātīvus*.

conversation.text: I'd like to speak to a representative, please.
I kept saying "representative" until the system connected me to a person.
A sales representative will call you within one business day.

senses.definition: To repay (a debt owed); specifically, to recompense or reward someone for (a favor, a service rendered, etc.)
senses.example: I hope to requite my debt to the bank by paying off the remaining balance next spring.

senses.definition: To repay (someone) a debt owed; specifically, to recompense or reward (someone) for a favor, a service rendered, etc.
senses.example: Our neighbors helped us move, and we vowed to requite their kindness someday.

senses.definition: To respond to or reciprocate (feelings, especially affection or love which has been shown).
senses.example: She did not requite his affection, so he eventually stopped sending her flowers.

senses.definition: To do or give a thing in return for (something).
senses.example: She wanted to requite his generous gift with a homemade pie.

senses.definition: To retaliate or seek revenge for (an insult, a wrong, etc.). to avenge.
senses.example: The old king swore to requite the insult that his rival had shouted in public.

senses.definition: To greet (someone) in return.
To make up for (something); to compensate.
senses.example: Extra hours at the office did little to requite the years he had missed at home.

senses.definition: To respond to (a question, a statement, etc.).
senses.example: He paused for a moment before he attempted to requite her pointed question.

senses.definition: To take the place of (someone or something); to replace.
senses.example: A new software library will requite the outdated module that our team has used for years.

senses.definition: Of an action, a quality, etc.: to be a reward for (itself).
senses.example: Hard work should requite itself, though in practice it often goes unnoticed.

senses.definition: To recompense, to repay.
To retaliate, to seek revenge.
senses.example: Grieving the loss, he vowed to requite, brooding on the betrayal for years.

senses.definition: (rare) To retaliate or seek revenge against (someone) for an insult, a wrong, etc. also, to seek revenge for (oneself).
senses.example: The jilted widow sought to requite her husband's mistress by ruining her reputation.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Chiefly in the form in requite for or of: synonym of requital (“compensation for damage or loss; return in kind, recompense, repayment, reward”).
senses.example: They offered a small payment in requite for the damaged fence.

core.definition: To repay someone for a kindness or wrong, or to return someone's feelings, especially love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The vowel is the diphthong 'eye', and the final 't' is a clear, light stop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing love or kindness; negative when describing revenge.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'requite' is literary and rare. It appears in poetry, novels and formal writing, often in phrases like 'requite love' or 'requite a favor'. In everyday speech people say 'return', 'repay' or 'pay back'.

distinctions.note: 'Repay' is the everyday word for returning money or favors; 'requite' is formal and can refer to feelings or revenge.
'Reciprocate' means to return in kind; 'requite' is more literary and often used for love or wrongs.

examples.everyday: I'd love to requite your help by buying you lunch next week.
examples.professional: Our team wants to requite the customers who stayed loyal during the outage with a service credit.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's sonnets ask whether a beloved can ever requite the speaker's devotion equally.

nuance.analogy: To requite is like returning a ball that was thrown to you: you send back what came your way.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'back' plus Middle English quit 'to repay', from Latin quietus 'at rest, free'.
common_mistakes: Using 'requite' as an everyday word for 'repay'; in conversation, say 'pay back'.
Confusing 'requite' with 'require', which looks similar but means to need or demand.

requite.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *requiten* (“to repay”), and then partly from both of the following:

senses.definition: The act of restricting, or the state of being restricted.
senses.example: The new lease includes a restriction on subletting without written approval from the landlord.

senses.definition: A regulation or limitation that restricts.
senses.example: The school has a strict restriction against bringing phones into the testing rooms.

senses.definition: The mechanism by which a cell degrades foreign DNA material.
senses.example: Bacteria rely on restriction systems to chop up invading viral DNA before infection spreads.

core.definition: A rule, limit or condition that controls what is allowed, or the act of limiting something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRIK, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'. Americans make the middle vowel a weak 'ih' sound, so do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it describes a limit, which people may see as helpful or as unfair depending on the situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use restriction in everyday talk for rules such as age or carry-on limits, and in news and policy writing for government or corporate limits. In casual speech, people often say 'rule', 'limit' or 'requirement'. Be aware that restrictions on speech or travel can be a politically heated topic.

distinctions.note: A limit is a maximum amount or boundary, while a restriction is a rule that controls what can be done.
A rule guides behavior in general, while a restriction specifically limits or narrows what is allowed.

examples.everyday: There are restrictions on carry-on liquids at the airport, so I put my shampoo in the checked bag.
examples.professional: The new data policy has restrictions on who can export customer records, so we need an approval step.
examples.analytical: Such restrictions on speech demand a strong justification in any free society, and the burden of proof should fall on the state.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence around a yard, a restriction marks the edge of what is allowed without stopping everything inside.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin restrictio, from restringere, 'to draw back, bind tight'.
common_mistakes: Using restriction with the wrong preposition: say 'restriction on' something, not 'restriction of' when you mean a limit on an activity.
Confusing restriction with restraint; restriction is a rule, while restraint is self-control or physical holding back.
Forgetting that restriction in biology, such as restriction enzymes, is a technical sense and not used in everyday talk.

restriction.etymology: From Middle English *restriccioun*, from Anglo-Norman *restriction*, Middle French *restriction*, and their source, Late Latin *restrictiō*, from Latin *restringō*.

senses.definition: Secluded from society (of a lifestyle, activity etc.); private, quiet.
senses.example: I lead a retired lifestyle.

senses.definition: Of a place, far from civilization, not able to be easily seen or accessed; secluded.
senses.example: They lived in a retired cabin at the end of a gravel road.

senses.definition: Having left employment, especially on reaching pensionable age.
senses.example: The retired workers are a major expense due to their pensions.

senses.definition: No longer in use or production.
senses.example: Following Jackie Robinson's success, his uniform number, 42, became a retired number across all major league teams.

core.definition: No longer working, having permanently left one's job, especially on reaching pension age.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIRED, which is one syllable with an r-colored vowel. Americans do not say three syllables like 'ri-TAI-ud', and the final d is clearly voiced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a status and is often used with warmth, though it can imply a loss of role or identity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'retired' before a profession as a title or identity, for example 'my retired neighbor' or 'a retired police officer'. Adding 'semi-' or 'partly' is common for people who still work part-time. For someone who holds a title after leaving, Americans often say 'former' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Former' means previously holding a role, but it does not say the person left at the end of a career, while 'retired' implies a permanent end to working life.
Emeritus is a formal academic title given to retired professors, while retired is the general word and applies to any profession.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is retired, so he's always out on his porch in the morning waving at everybody.
examples.professional: She is a retired Army officer who now consults for our defense analytics team on logistics planning.
examples.analytical: Sociologists ask whether a retired person's identity remains tied to their former profession, or whether a new role replaces it.

nuance.analogy: Being retired is like a play that has finished its run: the story is complete, and the actors now have different roles.
nuance.etymology: From retire, with the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'retired' as three syllables, 'ri-TAI-erd'.
Saying 'I am retiring' when you mean 'I have retired'; 'retiring' describes a process or a personality.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, reverts.
senses.example: The wiki's most active revert is a volunteer who undoes vandalism every single day.

senses.definition: One who reverts to that religion which one had adhered to before having converted to another.
senses.example: After years as a Lutheran, she became a revert to the Catholic faith of her childhood.

senses.definition: A convert to Islam.
senses.example: Several American reverts to Islam spoke at the community center's Friday prayer gathering.

senses.definition: The act of reversion (of e.g. a database transaction or source control repository) to an earlier state.
senses.example: We've found that git reverts are at least an order of magnitude faster than SVN reverse merges.

senses.definition: The skateboard maneuver of rotating the board 180 degrees or more while the wheels remain on the ground.
senses.example: She landed a clean revert off the curb, spinning the board a full 180 degrees before rolling away.

senses.definition: To throw back; to reflect; to reverberate. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The canyon walls revert the thunder, so it rolls back across the valley for minutes.

senses.definition: To cause to return to a former condition.
To reverse (a change).
senses.example: If the new policy fails, we will revert to the old schedule next month.

senses.definition: To reverse a change made by (a person).
senses.example: Please don't revert my edits again without explaining why in the discussion thread.

senses.definition: To return to the possession of.
senses.example: When a book goes out of print, rights revert from the publisher to the author.

senses.definition: Of an estate: To return to its former owner, or to his or her heirs, when a grant comes to an end.
senses.example: When the life tenant died, the land would revert to the original owner's heirs.

senses.definition: To cause (a property or rights) to return to the previous owner.
senses.example: Sometimes a publisher will automatically revert rights back to an author once a book has gone out of print.

senses.definition: To return to a former practice, condition, belief, etc.
To change back, as from a soluble to an insoluble state or the reverse.
senses.example: Phosphoric acid in certain fertilizers reverts.

senses.definition: To convert to Islam.
senses.example: After months of study, he decided to revert to Islam at the mosque downtown.

senses.definition: To treat (a series, such as y=a+bx+cx2+⋯, where one variable y is expressed in powers of a second variable x), so as to find the second variable x expressed in a series arranged in powers of y.
senses.example: To find the inverse series, we revert the power series so that x is expressed in powers of y.

senses.definition: To return to an earlier or primitive type or state; to take on the traits or characters of an ancestral type.
senses.example: Under stress, the crossbred plants began to revert to their wild ancestors' traits.

senses.definition: (rare) To turn back, or turn to the contrary; to reverse.
senses.example: Her mood would revert without warning, turning cheerful speech into bitter silence.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To return; to come back.
senses.example: If they attack, we will revert to the bunker.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To return to a former condition, practice, or state, often one that was abandoned or dropped.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VURT, with a strong American r and no extra vowel after it. The final t is a clear, light t, not a flap, because it ends the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can sound negative when describing a return to bad habits and positive when describing a return to a better setting. The religious sense, about someone returning to a faith, is sensitive and should be used carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say revert to with a noun, such as revert to the old settings or revert to old habits, and in casual speech they often say go back to. Revert back is common but redundant. In software, to revert a change means to undo it. In religious contexts, some Muslims find the term revert to Islam offensive and prefer convert, so avoid it unless you know the speaker's preference.

distinctions.note: Return is the general word for coming back to a place or state. Revert specifically implies going back to something earlier that was left behind.
Regress means moving to a worse or earlier stage of development, while revert is a broader return to a former state, good or bad.

examples.everyday: After a week of early nights, I reverted to staying up until midnight reading.
examples.professional: If the new build crashes, the system will revert to the last stable version automatically.
examples.analytical: The argument reverts to the same premise at the end, which makes the conclusion circular.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that returns to its old channel after a flood recedes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin revertere, to turn back, from re- back plus vertere, to turn.
common_mistakes: Saying revert back, which repeats the idea of back; say revert to.
Using revert with a person as subject to mean return home; it means return to a state or practice.

revert.etymology: From Old French *revertir*, from Vulgar Latin **revertiō*, variant of Latin *revertō*.

senses.definition: Synonym of off the bat.
senses.example: Right off the bat, the new manager made it clear that missed deadlines would not be tolerated.

core.definition: Immediately, from the very start, before anything else happens.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BAT, and right and off get lighter stress. Link the words smoothly: right-awf-thuh-BAT, with the t in right lightly flapped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it often suggests speed or surprise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in conversation and sports talk: 'He got the answer right off the bat.' A natural reply is 'Nice, you caught on fast.' It is too casual for formal writing, though it can appear in business emails.

distinctions.note: Same meaning; the version with right is slightly more emphatic.
From the start is plain and neutral; right off the bat adds a sense of speed and surprise.

collocations: had problems right off the bat

examples.everyday: We hit it off right off the bat, like we'd known each other for years.
examples.professional: The new hire impressed the team right off the bat with her clear questions.
examples.analytical: Right off the bat, the author's argument needs a clearer definition of consent before it can be evaluated.

nuance.analogy: Like a pitch that reaches the plate before the batter can move, it arrives immediately.
nuance.etymology: From baseball, where the bat is the first thing that comes into play when a pitch is thrown.
common_mistakes: Writing right of the bat instead of right off the bat.
Using it for slow progress; it always means immediately or from the very beginning.

conversation.text: Right off the bat, I knew we'd be friends.
The client asked about pricing right off the bat.
Right off the bat, the new system saved us an hour a day.

senses.definition: A person whose job is to rivet.
senses.example: Rosie the Riveter is an iconic piece of American WWII propaganda.

senses.definition: A gunner; the member of a riveting team who uses a rivet gun, fitted with a rivet set which matches the shape of the factory head of a solid rivet, to impact that rivet (which is heated if necessary to soften it), while the bucker (or holder-up) holds a heavy bucking bar against the bucktail of the rivet, upsetting it to form the field head. If the rivets have to be heated, the team will also include a cook and a catcher; see rivet for more details. Riveting team working on an aircraft cockpit shell. The riveter on the left operates an air-powered rivet gun, while the bucker on the right holds a bucking bar.
senses.example: Rosie the Riveter is an iconic piece of American WWII propaganda.

senses.definition: A tool used to fix rivets.
senses.example: The riveter required a compressed air supply.

core.definition: A worker whose job is to join metal parts with rivets, usually using a rivet gun or hammer.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, so RIV is strong and the second and third syllables are weak. The final syllable is a reduced r-colored schwa, so it sounds like er, not ayr.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
