nuance.usage_note: Riveter is an occupational term used in factories, shipyards and aircraft plants. Americans also remember Rosie the Riveter, the World War II poster figure symbolizing women in wartime industry. The word is rarely used in casual conversation outside those settings.

distinctions.note: A riveter joins metal with mechanical fasteners, while a welder fuses metal by melting it.
A fabricator shapes and assembles metal parts broadly, while a riveter specializes in riveted joints.

examples.everyday: My grandfather worked as a riveter at the shipyard during the war.
examples.professional: The plant is hiring two riveters for the wing assembly line next month.
examples.analytical: The riveter's skill lies in balancing the bucking bar and the rivet gun so the field head forms cleanly.

nuance.analogy: A riveter is like a stitcher in a metal shop, sewing parts together with hard steel pins instead of thread.
nuance.etymology: Formed from rivet, from Old French rivet meaning small nail, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as ree-ter or ri-VET-er instead of a reduced er.
Confusing riveter with welder, since both join metal in factories.

senses.definition: To revolve by turning over and over; to move by turning on a horizontal axis; to impel forward with a revolving motion on a supporting surface.
senses.example: To roll a wheel, a ball, or a barrel.

senses.definition: To wrap (something) round on itself; to form into a spherical or cylindrical body by causing to turn over and over.
senses.example: To roll a sheet of paper; to roll clay or putty into a ball.

senses.definition: To bind or involve by winding, as with a bandage; to enwrap; often with up.
senses.example: To roll up the vase in bubble wrap.

senses.definition: To drive, impel, or flow onward with a steady, wave-like motion.
senses.example: This river will roll its waters to the ocean.

senses.definition: To pour or trickle.
senses.example: Drops of sweat rolled down his face.

senses.definition: To utter copiously, especially with sounding words; to utter with a deep sound; — often with forth, or out.
senses.example: To roll forth someone's praises; to roll out sentences.

senses.definition: To press, level, spread, or form with a roller or rollers.
senses.example: to roll a field; to roll paste; to roll steel rails.

senses.definition: To move upon rollers or wheels.
To tumble in gymnastics; to do a somersault.
senses.example: The gymnast will roll forward off the balance beam and land on the mat.

senses.definition: To leave or begin a journey; sometimes with out.
senses.example: I want to get there early; let's roll.

senses.definition: To compete, especially with vigor.
senses.example: OK guys, we're only down by two points. Let's roll!

senses.definition: To walk, especially leisurely or idly; to stroll.
senses.example: Let's roll around town on foot and see the sights.

senses.definition: To beat with rapid, continuous strokes, as a drum; to sound a roll upon.
senses.example: The drummer began to roll on the snare, building tension before the final crash.

senses.definition: To apply (one line or surface) to another without slipping; to bring all the parts of (one line or surface) into successive contact with another, in such a manner that at every instant the parts that have been in contact are equal.
senses.example: In calculus, a wheel can roll along the ground without slipping at any point.

senses.definition: To turn over in one's mind, as of deep thoughts; to (cause to) be considered thoroughly.
senses.example: She wanted to roll the decision over in her mind before answering the letter.

senses.definition: To behave in a certain way; to adopt a general disposition toward a situation.
senses.example: I was going to kick his ass, but he wasn't worth getting all worked up over; I don't roll like that.

senses.definition: To throw dice.
senses.example: If you roll doubles, you get an extra turn.

senses.definition: To roll dice such that they form a given pattern or total.
senses.example: If you roll doubles, you get an extra turn.

senses.definition: To create a new character in a role-playing game, especially by using dice to determine properties.
senses.example: I'm gonna go and roll a new shaman tonight.

senses.definition: To generate a random number.
senses.example: Our script will roll a random number between one and six for each simulated player.

senses.definition: To perform an operation similar to a bit shift, but with the bit that "falls off the end" being wrapped around to the other end.
senses.example: To rotate the bits, the processor will roll the register left by three positions.

senses.definition: To travel by sailing.
senses.example: We planned to roll down the coast to Maine before the autumn storms arrived.

senses.definition: To beat up; to assault.
senses.example: Two men tried to roll him in the alley, but a passing officer stopped them.

senses.definition: To (cause to) betray secrets or testify for the prosecution.
senses.example: The feds rolled him by giving him a free pass for most of what he'd done.

senses.definition: To be under the influence of MDMA (a psychedelic stimulant, also known as ecstasy).
senses.example: Half the crowd at the festival was rolling, dancing until dawn.

senses.definition: To (cause to) film.
senses.example: The cameras are rolling.

senses.definition: To slip past (a defender) with the ball.
senses.example: He rolled past two defenders and finished the layup with his left hand.

senses.definition: To have a rolling aspect.
senses.example: the hills rolled on

senses.definition: To make a loud or heavy rumbling noise.
senses.example: The thunder rolled and the lightning flashed.

senses.definition: To utter with an alveolar trill.
senses.example: Many languages roll their r's.

senses.definition: To enrobe in toilet-paper (as a prank or spectacle).
senses.example: The kids rolled the principal's house and yard.

senses.definition: To create a customized version of; often followed by one's own.
senses.example: She rolled her own version of the open-source editor to fit her team's workflow.

senses.definition: To engage in sparring in the context of jujitsu or other grappling disciplines.
senses.example: After class, the two students rolled on the mats for twenty minutes.

senses.definition: To load ocean freight cargo onto a vessel other than the one it was meant to sail on.
senses.example: Containers will be rolled to another mother vessel.

senses.definition: To drum on the reverse of a game controller with one's fingers in rapid succession, pushing the controller face into the opposite hand such that a button is rapidly pressed and depressed.
senses.example: He rolled the controller in his hands to mash the buttons faster during the fight.

senses.definition: To rotate about the fore-and-aft axis, causing its sides to go up and down. Compare pitch, yaw.
senses.example: In a turn, the pilot had to roll the plane while keeping the nose level.

senses.definition: To briskly arpeggiate (a chord), typically in an upward motion.
senses.example: The pianist would roll the chord quickly, so the notes ring out together.

senses.definition: The act or result of rolling, or state of being rolled.
senses.example: the roll of a ball

senses.definition: Something formed into a compact shape by being rolled up.
senses.example: a roll of banknotes

senses.definition: A forward or backward roll in gymnastics; going head over heels. A tumble.
senses.example: The gymnast finished her routine with a perfect backward roll onto the mat.

senses.definition: Something which rolls.
senses.example: to pass rails through the rolls

senses.definition: A heavy cylinder used to break clods.
One of a set of revolving cylinders, or rollers, between which metal is pressed, formed, or smoothed, as in a rolling mill.
senses.example: to pass rails through the rolls

senses.definition: A swagger or rolling gait.
A heavy, reverberatory sound.
senses.example: Hear the roll of cannon.

senses.definition: The uniform beating of a drum with strokes so rapid as scarcely to be distinguished by the ear.
The rotation angle about the longitudinal axis.
senses.example: Calculate the roll of that aircraft.

senses.definition: An instance of the act of rolling an aircraft through one or more complete rotations about its longitudinal axis.
senses.example: The pilots entertained the spectators at the airshow by doing multiple rolls.

senses.definition: The act of, or total resulting from, rolling one or more dice.
senses.example: Make your roll.

senses.definition: A winning streak of continuing luck, especially at gambling.
senses.example: He is on a roll tonight.

senses.definition: A training match for a fighting dog.
An instance of the act of righting a canoe or kayak which has capsized, without exiting the watercraft, or being assisted.
senses.example: That was a good roll.

senses.definition: The skill of righting a canoe or kayak which has capsized, without exiting the watercraft, or being assisted.
senses.example: She has a bombproof roll.

senses.definition: Any of various financial instruments or transactions that involve opposite positions at different expiries, "rolling" a position from one expiry to another.
An operation similar to a bit shift, but with the bit that "falls off the end" being wrapped around to the other end.
A 14-day deployment.
That which is rolled up.
senses.example: a roll of fat, of wool, paper, cloth, etc.

senses.definition: A document written on a piece of parchment, paper, or other materials which may be rolled up; a scroll.
An official or public document; a register; a record.
A catalog or list, one kept for official purposes.
senses.example: The roll of solicitors contains the names of all admitted solicitors of a jurisdiction.

senses.definition: A food preparation comprising one or more ingredients wrapped in, e.g. flatbread, lettuce leaf, etc.
A quantity of cloth wound into a cylindrical form.
senses.example: a roll of carpeting; a roll of ribbon

senses.definition: A cylindrical twist of tobacco.
A kind of shortened raised biscuit or bread, often rolled or doubled upon itself; see also bread roll.
A measure of parchments, containing five dozen.

The oscillating movement of a nautical vessel as it rotates from side to side, about its fore-and-aft axis, causing its sides to go up and down, as distinguished from the alternate rise and fall of bow and stern called pitching; or the equivalent in an aircraft.
The measure or extent to which a vessel rotates from side to side, about its fore-and-aft axis.

core.definition: To move by turning over and over on a surface, like a ball or wheel, or to wrap something into a cylinder or ball.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with the 'oh' diphthong and a clear final l. Do not say 'rawl' or 'rool'; it rhymes with 'hole' and 'role'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the meaning depends on context and can be positive, as in 'let's roll', or negative, as in 'roll over someone'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'roll' in many everyday phrases, such as 'roll down the window', 'let's roll' meaning let's go, and 'roll with it' meaning accept a situation. In restaurants, 'roll' usually means a bread bun, so say 'dinner roll' to be clear. The word is extremely common in conversation.

distinctions.note: Spin means turning around a fixed axis in place; roll means moving forward while turning along a surface.
Turn is general; roll specifically suggests rotating over and over, like a ball or wheel.
Tumble implies falling or uncontrolled movement; roll is more controlled or continuous.

examples.everyday: Can you roll down the window? It's hot in here.
examples.professional: Let's roll out the new dashboard to the sales team next week.
examples.analytical: The argument rolls forward from one premise to the next, but never checks whether the first premise is true.

nuance.analogy: Like a snowball gathering as it rolls down a hill.
nuance.etymology: From Old French rouler, from Late Latin rotulare, from Latin rotulus, a small wheel or roll.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'roll' (to turn over) with 'roll' (a bread bun) and with the homophone 'role'.
Using 'roll' for quick movement without turning; a car rolls only when it moves on its wheels.

roll.etymology: From Middle English *rollen*, partly from Old French *roller*, *roler*, *röeler*, *röoler*, from Medieval Latin *rotulāre* (“to roll; to revolve”), from Latin *rotula* (“a little wheel”), diminutive of *rota* (“a wheel”); partly from Anglo-Latin *rollāre*,…

senses.definition: An operation which returns a database, or group of records in a database, to a previous state (normally to the previous commit point).
senses.example: The engineers initiated a rollback after the faulty update crashed the production database.

senses.definition: A return to a prior state by undoing some operation, especially of policy or price changes.
A withdrawal of military forces.
senses.example: The rollback of troops from the border region began in early spring.

senses.definition: The situation where a rollercoaster fails to reach the top of a hill and instead rolls backward.
senses.example: The coaster's rollback on the steep hill frightened the riders, who screamed as they slid backward.

senses.definition: A form of flatbed truck adapted or designed specifically to carry other vehicles, for use in recovery (wrecking, salvage) or for transporting.
senses.example: The tow company dispatched a rollback to haul the wrecked sedan off the interstate.

senses.definition: The strategy of forcing a change in the major policies of a state, usually by replacing its ruling regime, or by totally annihilating an enemy's armed forces and occupying the country, as was done in World War II to Italy, Germany, and Japan.
senses.example: Critics argued that the rollback of the regime would require occupying the country for years.

senses.definition: An uncommanded reduction in the thrust of a jet engine.
senses.example: Pilots reported a rollback in the left engine's thrust shortly after takeoff.

senses.definition: To return to the previous state.
senses.example: The server is unstable, we need to rollback the changes.

senses.definition: To reduce thrust without having been commanded to do so.
senses.example: The engine started to rollback during climb, so the crew reduced power manually.

core.definition: A reversal of a previous change, such as a price increase, a policy, or a database update, returning things to an earlier state.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ROHL, and make the second syllable a short, sharp 'bak.' Americans link the two parts with a light secondary stress, so avoid two equal stresses.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in business or politics it can be positive or negative depending on whether the change is welcome.
nuance.usage_note: In American news and business, rollback often describes a government or company undoing a policy or price increase, as in 'a rollback of tariffs.' In software and databases it refers to undoing changes to restore an earlier state. As a verb, roll back is common in both contexts, such as 'We rolled back the update.'

distinctions.note: Reversal is a broader and more general term for any change in direction, while rollback implies returning to a previous specific state.
Undo is an everyday command or action that reverses one step, while rollback often refers to restoring a whole system or set of changes.

examples.everyday: The store announced a rollback on gas prices, so the signs out front were changed this morning.
examples.professional: If the deployment fails, the engineering team will initiate a rollback to the last stable build.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the rollback of civil rights protections reflected shifting political priorities rather than new evidence.

nuance.analogy: A rollback is like pressing rewind on a video so the story returns to an earlier scene.
nuance.etymology: From roll (verb) plus back, meaning to return to an earlier position.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words 'roll back' when used as a noun in technical writing.
Using rollback for a new improvement instead of a reversal.
patterns: a rollback to sth (an earlier version)

senses.definition: To treat (someone) extremely well.
senses.example: The manager royal-treated the visiting author, arranging a limousine and a private dinner.

core.definition: Very special, generous treatment, as if you were a king or queen.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TREAT in 'treatment', and 'royal' is weaker. The final syllable '-ment' is reduced, and the two words link smoothly: 'ROY-uhl TREET'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warm hospitality and special attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'give someone the royal treatment' or 'get the royal treatment' for being treated extremely well, especially in hotels, restaurants and when hosting guests. A natural reply is 'Thanks, you really made me feel special.' The phrase is not literal, though it can sound ironic if the treatment was poor.

distinctions.note: VIP treatment is a modern, marketing-style phrase, while royal treatment has an old-fashioned hospitality feel.
Red-carpet treatment emphasizes public welcome at events, while royal treatment focuses on personal, lavish care.
Special treatment can mean unfair favoritism, while royal treatment is usually a warm compliment.

collocations: the royal treatment at the hotel

examples.everyday: The waiter gave us the royal treatment, refilling our water and bringing extra bread without our asking.
examples.professional: Our sales team wants to give key accounts the royal treatment during the onboarding week.
examples.analytical: Scholars of hospitality note that the royal treatment is less about luxury than about making a guest feel recognized.

nuance.analogy: Like a hotel where every door opens before you reach it: you feel like a monarch, and no request seems like a bother.
nuance.etymology: 'Royal' comes from Latin regalis (of a king); the phrase is a figurative use of 'royal' with 'treatment'.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on 'royal' instead of on TREAT in 'treatment'
Using the phrase as a verb on its own; say 'give someone the royal treatment' rather than 'royal treat someone'

senses.definition: A reply to an invitation.
senses.example: Please send your RSVP by Friday so we can finalize the catering order.

senses.definition: Initialism of rapid serial visual presentation.
senses.example: In our EEG study, each word was shown using RSVP at a fixed rate.

senses.definition: To reply to an invitation.
To reserve a place.
senses.example: Please RSVP for the workshop now, since seats are limited to thirty people.

senses.definition: Initialism of reserve seating via phone.
senses.example: The invitation said RSVP by phone, so I called the venue Monday.

core.definition: To reply to an invitation saying whether you will attend, usually by a given date.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters, with the strongest stress on the final 'P' sound: 'ar, ess, vee, PEE'. Don't pronounce it as a single word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to polite; it is a standard request on invitations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans write 'RSVP' on wedding and party invitations to ask guests to reply. Saying 'Please RSVP' is normal and polite. A natural reply is 'Yes, we'll be there' or 'Sorry, we can't make it.' The phrase comes from French 'répondez s'il vous plaît,' meaning please reply.

distinctions.note: 'Reply' is general; 'RSVP' specifically asks for a yes or no about attending an event.
'Regrets' means you are saying you cannot attend; it is a polite negative reply.

examples.everyday: Can you RSVP for the barbecue by Friday so my husband knows how much food to buy?
examples.professional: Please RSVP to the vendor meeting by Wednesday so we can reserve the conference room.
examples.analytical: The formal invitation asks guests to RSVP, which signals a social obligation to reply promptly.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign-up sheet for a potluck, where every guest has to put their name down.
nuance.etymology: From French 'répondez s'il vous plaît,' meaning 'please reply'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'RSVP' as one word like 'RSVP-ee'.
Forgetting to reply after receiving an invitation that asks for an RSVP.

conversation.text: Don't forget to RSVP for the wedding by Friday.
"Did you RSVP?" "Yeah, I said we'd both come."
Only half the guests RSVP'd, so we don't know how much food to buy.

senses.definition: The stage during which a program is executing.
The amount of time during which a program is executing.
A software component designed to support the execution of computer programs.
senses.example: You need to install the .NET runtime before you can run this application.

senses.definition: The length of a film, television program or audio track in minutes, usually with end credits included.
senses.example: Check the run time before you schedule the screening, since credits add several minutes.

core.definition: In software, the stage when a program is executing, or the period of time during which it runs, as opposed to when it is compiled.

pronunciation.tip: Compound nouns put the main stress on the first word, so RUN is strongest and time is weaker.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American software engineering, runtime is usually written as one word, though run time with a space appears in older texts and some documentation. Americans say running time for the length of a movie or event, so do not use run time for a film. In code and bug reports, runtime errors happen during execution, and developers talk about reducing runtime or memory usage.

distinctions.note: Compile time is when source code is translated into executable form; runtime is when the program is actually running.
Uptime is how long a system has been available and working; runtime is how long a particular program executes.
Execution time and runtime are close in meaning, but execution time usually refers to the measured duration of a specific task.

examples.everyday: My laptop got hot during the program's run time, so I closed a few tabs and it calmed down.
examples.professional: The runtime for the nightly batch job jumped from twenty minutes to forty after last night's deploy.
examples.analytical: Asymptotic analysis describes how the runtime of an algorithm grows with input size, deliberately abstracting away machine-specific constants.

nuance.analogy: Like the time a recipe spends in the oven, as opposed to the time you spent planning and shopping for ingredients.
nuance.etymology: Run from Old English rinnan; time from Old English tīma.
common_mistakes: Using run time for a movie's length; Americans say running time for films.
Writing run time in code documentation where runtime is the standard term.
Stressing time instead of RUN; the first word is the main stress in this compound noun.

senses.definition: A person who rushes.
The fast defensive position whose objective is to sack the offensive team's quarterback.
senses.example: The rusher broke through the line and hit the quarterback just as he threw the ball.

core.definition: A person who rushes or hurries toward something, or a defender who charges the quarterback in football.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RUSH. The second syllable is a weak schwa followed by a clear American r, so it sounds like RUSH-ur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In sports, a rusher is a positive or technical term for a player who pressures the offense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear rusher in football, where a defensive lineman or linebacker who charges the quarterback is called a pass rusher. In everyday speech the word is less common, and you might say someone who rushes or a person in a hurry instead. The football sense is so common that most Americans will think of it first.

distinctions.note: A blitzer is a defender who sends extra pressure, often from a different position, while a rusher is any player charging the quarterback.
Hurrier is rare and informal; rusher is the standard word for a person who moves in a rush.

examples.everyday: Our son is a good rusher on the high school football team, so he always gets the quarterback.
examples.professional: The coaching staff wants a stronger edge rusher on third downs.
examples.analytical: The quarterback's risk depends on how quickly the rusher closes the distance before the throw.

nuance.analogy: A pass rusher is like a sprinter at the starting line who bursts forward the moment the whistle blows.
nuance.etymology: From rush (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using rusher for any person in a hurry, which is understood but less natural than in a hurry or in a rush.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes it sound like a foreign word.

senses.definition: A person who regards and keeps the seventh day of the week ("Saturday", the Israelite or Jewish Sabbath) as holy in conformity with the fourth commandment of the Decalogue, such as an Orthodox Jew, Seventh-day Adventist, Seventh Day Baptist, a member of the Church of God (Seventh Day); a Sabbath-keeper, a Saturday-keeper.
senses.example: As a Sabbatarian, she worships on Sunday and rests on the first day of the week.

senses.definition: A person who regards and keeps the first day of the week as holy and often considers it as a replacement for the seventh-day Sabbath, a Sunday-keeper.
senses.example: As a Sabbatarian, she worships on Sunday and rests on the first day of the week.

senses.definition: A person who favors the strict observance of the Sabbath (either the sixth, seventh, or first day of the week).
senses.example: The old Sabbatarian in our town objected to any shopping on Sundays.

senses.definition: A member of a non-Jewish religious sect originating in Russia distinguished by observance of Jewish rites and festivals including Saturday as the day of rest.
senses.example: Historians describe the Sabbatarian community in nineteenth-century Russia as deeply devoted to Jewish rites.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the Sabbath, or the tenets of Sabbatarians.
senses.example: The church kept strict Sabbatarian rules, forbidding work from Saturday sunset until Sunday dawn.

core.definition: A person who observes a strict weekly Sabbath as a holy day of rest and worship, usually Saturday, but sometimes Sunday.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, TAIR, with the r pronounced clearly. Many learners wrongly stress the first syllable or drop the final -ian, which is an unstressed 'un' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a religious practice; some people use it to label strict believers and may sound judgmental, so it works best in neutral or academic talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in religious studies, church history, or discussions of Sabbath observance. Within a conversation, you would more often say 'Saturday-keeper' or name the denomination, such as Seventh-day Adventist. Sunday Sabbatarians, common among Puritans and some Presbyterians historically, are also called Sabbatarians, so check context before assuming which day is meant.

distinctions.note: A Seventh-day Adventist is a specific denomination that keeps Saturday holy; a Sabbatarian is anyone who keeps a strict weekly Sabbath, whatever their church.
Sabbatarian refers to religious observance of a holy day; sabbatical refers to a long, paid leave from work and has no religious meaning today.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a Seventh-day Adventist, so she's a Sabbatarian and won't do any shopping from Friday evening to Saturday night.
examples.professional: For the church history course, I'm writing a paper on how seventeenth-century English Sabbatarians shaped Sunday laws in New England.
examples.analytical: The Puritan Sabbatarian reading of the fourth commandment transferred Israel's seventh-day rest to the Lord's Day, a move that Lutheran and Anglican authors often questioned.

nuance.analogy: A Sabbatarian is like someone who reads a schedule so literally that they never change a single day on it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sabbatarius, from Sabbatum, the Sabbath, from Hebrew shabbat, 'rest'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (SAB-uh-tair-ee-un) instead of the third.
Confusing it with 'sabbatical', which means a long leave from work.
Assuming it always means Saturday keepers; Puritan Sabbatarians kept Sunday holy.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word shabbat means 'to cease' or 'rest', and it names the seventh day when God rested from creation (Genesis 2:2-3). Exodus 20:8-11 gives the fourth commandment to remember the sabbath and keep it holy, grounding the practice in creation and in Israel's deliverance. In Mark 2:27 Jesus teaches that the sabbath was made for man, so it serves human good rather than being a burden. Colossians 2:16 tells believers not to be judged over a sabbath, which early Christians used to debate whether Sabbath observance was binding on them.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church regards Sunday as the Lord's Day, the day of the Resurrection, and sees the Sabbath rest as fulfilled in Christ. Saturday has some liturgical significance, but strict Sabbath-keeping is not required.

The Catholic Church teaches that Sunday, the Lord's Day, is kept in honor of the Resurrection and carries a duty to attend Mass and rest from unnecessary work. It does not require the Jewish Saturday Sabbath.

Protestant views vary. Reformed and Puritan Sabbatarians held that the fourth commandment binds Christians to a strict Sunday Sabbath, while Lutherans and many Anglicans treat Sunday observance as a church ordinance rather than a command. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday as the Sabbath.

sabbatarian.etymology: From Medieval Latin *sabbatarius*, from Latin *sabbatum*, from Ancient Greek *σάββατον*, from Hebrew *an*.

senses.definition: Wise.
senses.example: She gave sage advice about saving money before buying the house.

senses.definition: A very wise person or spiritual teacher; someone of gravity and wisdom, especially, a teacher venerable for years, and of sound judgment and prudence; a grave or stoic philosopher.
senses.example: The village elders were regarded as sages who settled every dispute.

senses.definition: The plant Salvia officinalis, native to the Mediterranean region, widely grown as a herb and as an ornamental garden plant.
senses.example: Brown the butter with fresh sage leaves and pour it over the squash ravioli.

senses.definition: The dried leaves of Salvia officinalis, used as a herb in cooking.
Any plant in the genus Salvia.
senses.example: Hummingbirds visit the red sage in our garden every morning in June.

senses.definition: Any of a number of plants such as sagebrush considered to be similar to Salvia officinalis, mostly because they are small shrubs and have gray foliage or are aromatic.
senses.example: Sage covers the high desert hills of eastern Oregon for miles in every direction.

senses.definition: The foliage of sagebrush or similar plants.
senses.example: Cattle graze on sage in winter when grass is buried under snow.

senses.definition: Word used in the email field of imageboards to prevent a bump of the post. Used as an option rather than a word in some imageboard software.
senses.example: sage in all fields

senses.definition: The act of using the word or option sage in the email field or a checkbox of an imageboard when posting a reply.
senses.example: Reminder to sage and report.

core.definition: A common herb with gray-green, fuzzy leaves, used in cooking, especially with poultry, pork, stuffing and sausage.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds like "Say" plus a soft j, one syllable. Don't add an extra vowel between the sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American grocery stores and kitchens, sage usually means the dried or fresh herb, especially at Thanksgiving with turkey and stuffing. Americans also use the word for a wise older person, but in everyday talk the herb is more common. Online forums use a separate meaning, which is rare outside those communities.

distinctions.note: Basil is sweet and used in Italian dishes; sage is earthier and more savory, used in holiday cooking.
Same spelling, different meaning; context shows whether you mean the herb or a wise person.

examples.everyday: Can you pick up some fresh sage at the store for the turkey stuffing?
examples.professional: The restaurant's new menu uses brown butter with sage on the squash ravioli.
examples.analytical: In early modern herbals, sage was prized as a remedy, and its culinary use grew out of that medicinal reputation.

nuance.analogy: Sage in the kitchen is like the bay leaf in a soup: small in quantity, but it defines the flavor of the whole dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin salvia, from salvus, safe or healthy, referring to its medicinal reputation.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like "sadge" with a short a.
Confusing the herb with the adjective "sage" meaning wise, which is pronounced the same.

sage.etymology: From Middle English *sage*, from Old French *sage* (11th century), from Vulgar Latin **sapium*, from Latin *sapere* (“to taste, to discern, to be wise”).

senses.definition: Salt.
Shorea robusta, a dipterocarpaceous tree.
senses.example: The sal trees in the Himalayan foothills provide timber used for heavy construction.

core.definition: Salt, a word from Latin used in chemistry and some scientific names for certain salts.

pronunciation.tip: It is one short syllable with the vowel of cat and a clear l. It rhymes with pal and gal, so don't stretch it into a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In everyday English it is rare and may sound unfamiliar or like a name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say salt for the everyday substance and almost never use sal alone in conversation. You will see sal in scientific names such as sal ammoniac or sal soda. Sal is also a common nickname for Sally, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Salt is the everyday English word, while sal is a Latin word used mainly in chemistry and historical names.
Sal used as a proper noun is a nickname for Sally, not a word for salt, so the meaning depends on capitalization and context.

examples.everyday: My friend from Spain says sal means salt, so she told me to add some sal to the soup.
examples.professional: The chemical supply list includes sal ammoniac, an older name for ammonium chloride that still appears in some catalogs.
examples.analytical: The Latin word sal gave chemistry several names, such as sal ammoniac and sal soda, which preserve older naming systems.

nuance.analogy: Like an old label on a jar that still names the contents in the language of the workshop that made it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sal, meaning salt.
common_mistakes: Using sal as an everyday English word for table salt, where Americans say salt.
Confusing sal with the name Sal, which refers to a person and is capitalized.

core.definition: A man of the tribe of Judah, father of Boaz by Rahab, named in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew and Ruth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAM, and the l is silent, so the name sounds like SAM-un. Many non-native speakers pronounce the l, which Americans do not.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name of a biblical figure, with no emotional weight in ordinary speech.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches and Bible studies, Salmon is mentioned mainly when reading the genealogy of Jesus or the book of Ruth. Americans would normally say the name the same way as the fish, which can be confusing, so context matters. Salmon is a male name in the Bible, and it is not commonly used as a personal first name today.

distinctions.note: Zalmon, spelled with Z, is a place name, Mount Zalmon, in Judges 9:48 and Psalm 68:14, while Salmon is a person.
Salmon the fish is a common noun spelled in lowercase, while Salmon the biblical figure is a proper noun capitalized.

examples.everyday: During Bible study, our pastor pointed out that Salmon is in Jesus' family tree, which surprised a lot of people.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, the teacher noted that Salmon, Boaz and Rahab appear together in the lineage listed in Matthew 1.
examples.analytical: The inclusion of Salmon in the genealogy of Matthew, alongside the Gentile Rahab, underscores the inclusion of outsiders in the covenant line.

nuance.analogy: Salmon is like a name on a family tree that quietly connects the story of Ruth to the story of Jesus.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Salmon', a personal name meaning something like 'garment' or 'clothed', though the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the l in Salmon, which Americans never do.
Confusing the biblical man with the fish or with Zalmon, the mountain.
nuance.biblical_note: Salmon (Hebrew Salmon, sometimes spelled Salma) is a man of Judah and the father of Boaz, through whom David descended. Ruth 4:21 names him in the genealogy at the end of Ruth, and Matthew 1:4-5 lists him as the father of Boaz by Rahab in Jesus' ancestry. Luke 3:32 also includes Salmon in Jesus' genealogy, showing the family line of David and the inclusion of foreign women like Rahab and Ruth.

salmon.etymology: From Middle English *samoun*, *samon*, *saumon*, from Anglo-Norman *saumon*, from Old French *saumon*, from Latin *salmo*.

senses.definition: In AI safety, a model deliberately underperforming on an evaluation, for example to hide a dangerous capability.
Deliberately underperforming or setting low expectations so as to look better later or gain an advantage, as in sales targets, poker or golf.

core.definition: Deliberately underperforming to hide one's true ability; in AI safety, a model strategically doing worse on capability evaluations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SAND. Both a's are the flat American 'a' of 'cat', and the 'g' is fully pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies strategic deception.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, sandbagging means lowballing forecasts so you can beat them ('he's sandbagging his quarterly numbers'). AI safety researchers borrowed it for models that underperform on dangerous-capability evals, which would make safety testing unreliable. It is informal but standard in both settings.

distinctions.note: Reward hacking exploits flaws in the objective to score higher; sandbagging deliberately scores lower.
Deceptive alignment is the broader hypothesis of a model hiding misaligned goals; sandbagging is one specific behavior it might produce.
To underpromise is a usually harmless way to manage expectations; sandbagging implies hiding true ability for advantage.

examples.everyday: He says he's terrible at pool, but I think he's sandbagging so we'll bet on the game.
examples.professional: Our safety evals include checks for sandbagging, such as comparing scores with and without a hint that the test is an evaluation.
examples.analytical: If capable models can engage in sandbagging, a passed evaluation is weaker evidence of safety than it appears.

nuance.analogy: Sandbagging is the pool hustler's trick: miss easy shots until the stakes are high enough to matter.
nuance.etymology: From sandbag; the sense of feigning weakness to gain an advantage comes from American card-playing and sports slang.
common_mistakes: Using it for honest poor performance; sandbagging is always deliberate.

sandbagging.etymology: From *sandbag* (“to hit with a sandbag; to deceive by feigning weakness”) + *-ing*.

senses.definition: A coward; a person who is easily frightened or high-strung and easily scared.

core.definition: A person who is easily frightened or timid, usually said playfully, though it can sound insulting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'y' ending is a light 'ee' sound. The word 'cat' has a short 'a' as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Playful or mildly negative; it teases someone for being easily scared.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'scaredy-cat' casually, often with children or friends, and it is the most common form of this word. It can sting if used seriously toward an adult. Avoid it in formal or professional settings. A natural reply is 'Ha, maybe a little, but I still went in.'

distinctions.note: 'Scaredy-cat' is more common in American English, while 'scaredy pants' is less frequent and sounds slightly childish.
'Coward' is a stronger, more serious insult, while 'scaredy-cat' is informal and often playful.

examples.everyday: My little brother is such a scaredy-cat that he won't go into the basement alone.
examples.professional: I'm not a scaredy-cat about deployments, but I want a rollback plan before we push on Friday.
examples.analytical: Labeling critics as scaredy-cats is a rhetorical move that dismisses their concerns without engaging them.

nuance.analogy: A scaredy-cat is like a cat that bolts at every loud noise, even when nothing is there.
nuance.etymology: From 'scared' with the informal suffix '-y' and 'cat', a playful animal name for a timid person.
common_mistakes: Writing it without the hyphen, as 'scaredy cat', which is less standard.
Using it seriously toward adults in professional settings, where it can sound insulting.

senses.definition: Overly sentimental, emotional, maudlin or bathetic.

core.definition: Overly sentimental and emotional, in a way that feels forced, sweet or manipulative.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The 'lts' cluster is quick with no added vowel, and the final -y is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, though often used with a laugh and sometimes affectionately about a friend's favorite movie.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use schmaltzy for movies, songs, greeting cards, speeches and ads that feel too sweet or manipulative. It is casual, and people often say 'that's so schmaltzy' with a smile when a film gets sappy. For a more formal critique, say 'sentimental' or 'maudlin'.

distinctions.note: Sentimental can be sincere and admirable; schmaltzy implies the emotion is overdone or manufactured.
Maudlin is stronger and describes tearful self-pity; schmaltzy is lighter and focuses on sweetness.
Cheesy describes things that are corny or tacky, often in a funny way; schmaltzy focuses on exaggerated emotion.

examples.everyday: I love that movie, but the ending is so schmaltzy that I always roll my eyes.
examples.professional: The keynote was a bit schmaltzy, but the audience loved the customer stories.
examples.analytical: Dickens is often criticized as schmaltzy, yet his sentiment is tied to sharp social critique.

nuance.analogy: A schmaltzy story is like a greeting card that plays music: sweet, loud and a little too much.
nuance.etymology: From schmaltz, from Yiddish shmalts, from German Schmalz 'grease'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first.
Confusing the adjective with the food sense of schmaltz; schmaltzy is only about emotion.

senses.definition: Covered with or consisting of scrub.
senses.example: a scrubby landscape

senses.definition: Inferior in size or quality.
senses.example: scrubby crops

senses.definition: Diminutive of scrubber: a small scrubber for light washing tasks.
senses.example: dish scrubby

senses.definition: A loofah.
senses.example: She rinsed the scrubby under hot water before washing the bathtub.

core.definition: Small, stunted, or shabby; of poor quality or not very impressive in size or appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKRUB-ee. The final -y is a clear 'ee' sound, not 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests something small, cheap, or poorly kept, though it can be used mildly for plain, rough places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scrubby for low, stunted bushes or land, and for something cheap or shabby, such as a scrubby lawn or a scrubby little motel. It is not a polite word for a person's appearance, so for people say shabby or rough-looking. The noun meaning, a small scrubber or a loofah, is much less common in American speech.

distinctions.note: Shabby means worn out and neglected, while scrubby adds the idea of small, stunted, or low-quality growth or goods.
Scruffy describes an untidy look, especially of a person or animal, while scrubby describes size, quality, or low bushy land.

examples.everyday: We stayed at a scrubby little motel off the highway, but the beds were clean.
examples.professional: The vendor's scrubby prototype needs better parts before we show it to the client.
examples.analytical: The region's scrubby terrain, with its low and stunted vegetation, makes it poor for grazing and for farming.

nuance.analogy: Like a thin, cheap coat that barely keeps out the cold.
nuance.etymology: From scrub, meaning stunted low bushes, plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Calling a person scrubby to mean untidy; say scruffy or shabby instead.
Stressing the second syllable (skruh-BEE) instead of the first (SKRUB-ee).

senses.definition: Any bird that spends most of its time in coastal waters or over the oceans.

core.definition: A bird that spends most of its life on or over the ocean and comes to land mainly to nest, such as a gull, tern or puffin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SEE. The second syllable is an r-colored vowel like the ur in bird, so do not add an extra syllable or say sea-BIRD.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is often linked to nature, coastlines and wildlife.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seabird in nature writing, birdwatching, aquarium guides and talk about the beach. Casual speakers usually name the specific bird, such as gull or pelican, rather than saying seabird. The word is neutral and common on park signs and in conservation work.

distinctions.note: A shorebird, such as a sandpiper, feeds along the water's edge and on mudflats, rather than mainly far out at sea.
Waterbird is broader and includes ducks and herons that live on lakes and rivers, not only the ocean.

examples.everyday: We saw a flock of seabirds diving near the pier this morning.
examples.professional: The coastal project will protect nesting sites for seabirds that depend on fish from these waters.
examples.analytical: Seabirds are shaped by the sea, and their salt glands and long wings show how a life over open water demands special adaptations.

nuance.analogy: Like a sailor who rarely stays on land: the seabird lives on the water and comes ashore only to rest or nest.
nuance.etymology: Compound of sea and bird, from Old English sǣ and brid.
common_mistakes: Calling any bird near water a seabird; a duck on a lake is not a seabird.
Pronouncing bird with a short i sound, like bid.

senses.definition: Something used to add taste or flavor to food, such as salt and pepper or other condiment, herb or spice.
Anything added to increase enjoyment.
senses.example: The chili needed more seasoning, so I added cumin, salt, and a pinch of cayenne.

senses.definition: A coat of polymerized oil inside a cooking vessel which renders the surface non-stick.
senses.example: Keep the cast-iron skillet's seasoning intact by wiping it with oil after every use.

senses.definition: In diamond-cutting, the charging of the laps or wheels with diamond dust and oil.
senses.example: The diamond cutter prepared the wheels with diamond dust and oil before seasoning the lap.

senses.definition: The air drying of wood.
senses.example: The lumber needs at least a year of seasoning before the carpenter can use it.

core.definition: Salt, pepper, herbs, spices or other ingredients added to food to make it taste better.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like two syllables, not three. Don't pronounce the final -ing as -eeng.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes something that improves flavor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seasoning mostly for dry mixes like salt, pepper, garlic powder or a spice blend, and a cook might say the food needs more seasoning. In a restaurant, a server may ask whether you want extra seasoning, but at home people more often say spices or seasonings. Used figuratively, it means something that adds interest, as in a little humor is a good seasoning to a long meeting.

distinctions.note: A spice comes from seeds, bark, roots or fruit, such as cinnamon or cumin, while seasoning is the broader category that includes salt and herbs.
Flavor is the taste that food has; seasoning is what you add to create or improve that taste.

examples.everyday: This chicken needs a little more seasoning, so can you pass the salt?
examples.professional: Our test kitchen adjusted the seasoning in the sauce before the product launch.
examples.analytical: For Aristotle, the seasoning of a tragedy by pity and fear is not decoration but the means by which the audience is purified.

nuance.analogy: Seasoning is like the spotlight on a stage: it doesn't change the play, but it makes the important parts visible.
nuance.etymology: From season (verb), from Latin sationare, to sow or to salt food.
common_mistakes: Saying seasoning for a single item like pepper; say a spice or salt instead.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel; it is reduced in American speech.

conversation.text: This needs more seasoning; it's bland.
What seasoning did you put on the chicken?
I use a seasoning mix for tacos.

senses.definition: A thick oily substance, secreted by the sebaceous glands of the skin, that consists of fat, keratin and cellular debris.
senses.example: Oily seba builds up in the pores and can lead to breakouts on the forehead.

core.definition: The oily substance sebum, secreted by skin glands; seba is a nonstandard spelling of sebum.

pronunciation.tip: The correct word is sebum, with stress on the first syllable and a weak final syllable, 'bum'. Americans don't stress the second syllable, so avoid 'se-BUM'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise medical and cosmetic term.
nuance.usage_note: The headword should be spelled sebum. In American dermatology and skin care, people talk about excess sebum, oily skin, or clogged pores. In everyday speech, Americans usually say oily skin rather than the technical term.

distinctions.note: Sweat comes from sweat glands and is mostly water. Sebum comes from sebaceous glands and is oily.
Tallow is animal fat used for candles or soap. Sebum is the oil produced by human skin.

examples.everyday: My dermatologist said my oily skin comes from extra sebum, so I should wash my face twice a day.
examples.professional: The skincare formula targets sebum production without drying out the skin.
examples.analytical: Sebum's role in protecting the skin barrier is often overlooked in debates about acne treatment.

nuance.analogy: Sebum is the skin's natural lubricant, like the oil a mechanic applies so moving parts don't wear down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sebum, tallow or suet.
common_mistakes: Spelling the word seba instead of sebum.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'se-BUM'.

senses.definition: An intermediate person or means; intermediary.
senses.example: The news reached the mayor second hand, through a clerk who had heard it from a reporter.

senses.definition: On the clock face of a clock or watch, the hand (pointer) that shows the number of seconds that have passed.
senses.example: The second hand on my watch stopped, so I replaced the battery.

core.definition: The thin hand on a clock or watch that moves around the dial once a minute, showing seconds.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAND most strongly in this phrase, with the first word reduced to SEK-und. Do not confuse the two-word clock part with the one-word adjective secondhand, which is stressed on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical object with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the second hand' when talking about the clock or watch, as in 'Watch the second hand.' The spelling secondhand, one word, is an adjective meaning used or passed through others, as in secondhand car, or heard indirectly. Using the two-word form for the adjective is a common spelling mistake in writing.

distinctions.note: Secondhand (one word) is an adjective meaning used or indirect; second hand (two words) is the clock part.
The minute hand moves once an hour and shows minutes, while the second hand moves once a minute and shows seconds.

collocations: the second hand sweeps around the dial
the second hand on the wall clock
count the seconds by the second hand

examples.everyday: Can you watch the second hand and tell me when a full minute has passed?
examples.professional: Our old wall clock's second hand stuck, so the meeting timer kept freezing until someone replaced the battery.
examples.analytical: The sweep of the second hand divides time into equal discrete units, which makes a minute feel like a series of steps rather than a continuous flow.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner on a circular track who completes one lap every minute, marking each step as it passes.
nuance.etymology: From second (from medieval Latin secunda, 'second division of an hour') and hand.
common_mistakes: Writing secondhand as two words when you mean the clock part, or writing second hand as one word when you mean used.
Stressing the first word too strongly, which makes the phrase sound like a different word.

senses.definition: Something that lasts or takes a specified number of seconds.
senses.example: Each sensor reading was averaged over a seconder to smooth out noise.

senses.definition: The person who makes a second to a motion in any formal procedure, such as a parliamentary procedure.
senses.example: He's been the seconder on many motions, but I don't think he's ever made a motion himself.

senses.definition: A Cub Scout serving as a second-in-command to a sixer.
senses.example: The seconder took charge of the den while the sixer ran to get the first aid kit.

senses.definition: A person who seconds; a person who climbs after the leader.
senses.example: The seconder followed the lead climber up the icy ridge, clipping in at every bolt.

core.definition: The person who formally supports a motion so that it can be discussed or voted on in a meeting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is weak, like 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a procedural role without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in formal meetings, clubs, boards and student governments that follow Robert's Rules of Order. People more often say 'Is there a second?' or 'I'll second that' than call someone a seconder. The word is rarely heard outside meeting settings.

distinctions.note: The mover proposes a motion, while the seconder only agrees that it should be considered.
Supporter is a general term for anyone who backs an idea, while seconder names a formal procedural role.
An endorser publicly approves a candidate or product, not a motion in a meeting.

examples.everyday: Nobody wanted to be the seconder for my potluck idea, so it died right there at the table.
examples.professional: The chair asked for a seconder, and our VP stepped up to second the motion to approve the budget.
examples.analytical: A motion without a seconder dies on the floor, which shows that the procedure protects an assembly from acting on proposals no one else will support.

nuance.analogy: Like a co-signer on a loan: your name makes the request official enough to be considered.
nuance.etymology: From second, from Latin secundus, following, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable with an 'ah' vowel, as in 'sek-ahn-der'
Confusing seconder with the time unit 'second'
Saying 'I am a seconder' when the natural phrase is 'I second that'

senses.definition: A device used to plant seeds; a seed drill.
A person who sows seeds.
senses.example: My grandfather was a careful seeder, spacing each row of corn exactly as his father had taught him.

senses.definition: An implement used to remove the seeds from fruit etc.
senses.example: She used a melon seeder to scoop out the pulp and seeds before slicing the pumpkin.

senses.definition: A person who seeds clouds in order to make it rain.
senses.example: The state hired a cloud seeder to release silver iodide over the mountains during the drought.

senses.definition: A person connected to a peer-to-peer network who has a complete or partial copy of a given file and makes it available for downloading.
senses.example: Once the download hit one hundred percent, the seeder kept the file available for other users.

senses.definition: A process that seeds a random number generator.
senses.example: Before running the simulation, the analyst set the seeder to a fixed value so results could be reproduced.

senses.definition: A stamp-type leatherworking tool predominantly used in floral designs to represent the seeds in the center of a flower.
senses.example: She pressed the seeder into the damp leather to create tiny dots at the center of each rose.

core.definition: A machine that places seeds into the ground at a set depth and spacing, such as a planter or seed drill.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, seed, and the final -er is weak and rhotic, like the r in butter. Learners often stress the second syllable, saying see-DARE, which is incorrect.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical farming and landscaping term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seeder for lawn and pasture machines, especially when someone is overseeding a yard in the fall. Farmers may also say seed drill or planter, with drill meaning a machine that places seeds in neat rows. A person who sows seeds is usually called a sower, so seeder for a person sounds unusual.

distinctions.note: A seed drill places seeds in rows at controlled depth, while a seeder can also mean a lawn machine or a broadcast device.
A spreader scatters seed or fertilizer over an area, while a seeder places seeds more precisely into soil.

examples.everyday: I rented a lawn seeder from the hardware store to fix the bare patches in the backyard.
examples.professional: The seeder calibration is off, so the soybean rows are coming in too dense for the planned spacing.
examples.analytical: Jethro Tull's seed drill of the early eighteenth century made planting depth and spacing measurable, which shifted farming from broadcasting to row crops.

nuance.analogy: A seeder is like a pastry bag for the field: it places each seed at a controlled point rather than spraying them everywhere.
nuance.etymology: Seed plus the agent suffix -er, meaning a device or person that does the action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in see-DARE, instead of the first.
Using seeder to mean a person who plants seeds, where sower is the standard word.

seeder.etymology: From Middle English *seeder*, *seder*, from Old English *sǣdere* (“sower”), equivalent to *seed* + *er*.

senses.definition: Any set for which there is a binary operation that is closed and associative.

core.definition: In mathematics, a set with an associative binary operation that is closed under that operation, without requiring an identity or inverses.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEM. The second syllable is "ee," and the final "group" sounds like "groop," with a clear American r in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: American mathematicians use "semigroup" in abstract algebra courses and papers. It is never used in everyday speech. The term is a precise technical name, and in mathematics it is a weaker structure than a group.

distinctions.note: A group also requires an identity element and inverses for every element; a semigroup requires only closure and associativity.
A monoid is a semigroup with an identity element, but it need not have inverses.

examples.everyday: My brother studies math, and he said a semigroup is like a group that is missing a couple of rules.
examples.professional: For the cryptography project, we needed a semigroup that preserves the operation under composition.
examples.analytical: Every group is a semigroup, but the converse fails, since a semigroup need not contain inverses or an identity.

nuance.analogy: A semigroup is like a set of Lego connections where any two pieces can be joined in a consistent order, but there may be no blank piece and no way to undo a join.
nuance.etymology: Compound of "semi-" (half) and "group," from Latin semi- and English group.
common_mistakes: Confusing semigroup with group; a semigroup need not have identity or inverse elements.
Stressing the second syllable of "semi"; keep the stress on SEM.

semigroup.etymology: From *semi* + *group*, reflecting the fact that not all the conditions required for a group are required for a semigroup.

senses.definition: Of the physical senses or sensation.
Conveying nerve impulses from the sense organs to the nerve centers.
senses.example: sensory neurons

senses.definition: (dated) The sensorium.
senses.example: Early physiologists debated how the sensory registered pain, touch, and temperature in the brain.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Relating to the five physical senses or to the sensations they produce, such as sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable is 'ree', with an American 'r' sound that is clearly rhotic. Many non-native speakers add an extra vowel between the 's' and 'r'; keep the ending smooth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a descriptive term that is neither positive nor negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sensory' in science, medicine, design, and everyday talk about experiences, as in 'sensory overload' or 'sensory details' in writing. It is common in product descriptions and in discussions about autism or sensory processing. It is a neutral term, so it does not carry the erotic meaning of 'sensual'.

distinctions.note: Sensory is neutral and describes the physical senses, while sensual often implies erotic or indulgent pleasure.
Sensuous suggests aesthetic pleasure from beauty or texture, whereas sensory is a neutral technical description of the senses.

examples.everyday: The concert was amazing, but the lights and noise gave me sensory overload after an hour.
examples.professional: Our usability team ran sensory tests on the new packaging to see how customers rated its texture and smell.
examples.analytical: Locke treats sensory experience as the source of all simple ideas, which the mind then combines and reflects upon.

nuance.analogy: Sensory input is like the doorway of a house: everything that enters the mind from the outside world passes through it first.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sensorius, from Latin sensus 'feeling, perception', from sentire 'to feel'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sensory' with 'sensible' or 'sensitive' in sentences about the body or perception.
Using 'sensory' as a noun for a person's feelings; it is an adjective in most contexts.

senses.definition: Able to be separated.
Able to be brought to a form where all occurrences of the dependent and the independent variable are on opposite sides of the equal sign.
senses.example: The equation is separable, so we can move all y terms to one side.

senses.definition: Having a countable dense subset.
senses.example: A separable metric space has a countable dense subset, which simplifies the proof.

senses.definition: Any of several technical senses relating to the behavior of polynomials or objects over which polynomials can be defined:
senses.example: x2+1 is separable, since its roots are i and −i.

senses.definition: Having no repeated roots (where roots are considered in an algebraic closure)
senses.example: x2+1 is separable, since its roots are i and −i.

senses.definition: Such that the minimal polynomial of every element of E is a separable polynomial.
senses.example: Every element of the extension is separable over the base field, as the course proved.

senses.definition: Satisfying any of several technical conditions on the center of the algebra which generalize the situation of field extensions; see Separable algebra on Wikipedia.Wikipedia.
senses.example: A separable algebra over a field generalizes the idea of a separable field extension.

core.definition: Able to be separated or pulled apart into distinct parts, often without damaging the whole.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEP, and the word has three syllables. The middle syllable is a reduced ruh, so do not add an extra vowel as in sep-uh-RAB-ul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; positive when describing flexible or modular parts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use separable for things that come apart, such as removable parts, modular software or lids. In grammar, Americans call a phrasal verb separable when the particle can move away from the verb, as in turn the light off. For everyday objects, removable or detachable is often simpler.

distinctions.note: Detachable suggests a part that can be removed from a whole, like a hood on a jacket; separable is broader and can include abstract parts.
Distinct means recognizably different, but not necessarily able to be taken apart; separable means it can actually be split.

examples.everyday: The lid is separable, so you can take it off to wash the bowl.
examples.professional: Good design makes each feature separable, so we can ship one without rewriting the others.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a person's character is not separable from their actions, since the self is shaped by what it does.

nuance.analogy: Separable parts are like the layers of a cake that lift out one at a time without crumbling the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin separabilis, from separare, to separate.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in sep-uh-RAB-ul.
Confusing separable with separate, which is a verb or a different adjective.

separable.etymology: From Middle English *separable*, from Middle French *separable* and its etymon Latin *sēparābilis*.

senses.definition: Containing, secreting, or resembling serum; watery; a fluid or discharge that is pale yellow and transparent, usually representing something of a benign nature. (This contrasts with sanguine, which means blood-tinged and usually harmful.)
senses.example: The doctor said the drainage was serous, pale and clear, so the wound was healing well.

core.definition: Of or containing serum, the thin, pale yellow, watery fluid that separates from blood or tissue.

pronunciation.tip: It has two syllables: 'SEER' and 'us'. Do not say 'SAIR-us' and do not confuse it with 'serious', which has three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical description with no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'serous' mainly in medicine, nursing, and biology when describing fluid from wounds, membranes, or tissues. Laypeople usually say 'clear' or 'watery' fluid. In a clinical note, the word helps distinguish serous drainage from purulent (pus-filled) or bloody drainage.

distinctions.note: Serous is a medical term about fluid. Serious is an everyday adjective meaning grave or sincere. The two words sound similar but have no relation in meaning.
Sanguineous means blood-containing or blood-colored. Serous fluid is pale and watery, while sanguineous fluid is bloody.
Purulent means containing pus, which usually signals infection. Serous fluid is thin and pale, and it is not pus.

examples.everyday: The nurse said the drainage is serous, which is a good sign that the wound is healing.
examples.professional: Please document the wound as serous drainage rather than purulent in the chart, so the team knows it's not infected.
examples.analytical: The pericardium has a serous lining that secretes a thin fluid to reduce friction between the heart and surrounding tissues.

nuance.analogy: Like the thin film of oil that keeps two moving metal parts from grinding against each other.
nuance.etymology: From Latin serosus, from serum ('whey, watery fluid').
common_mistakes: Confusing 'serous' with 'serious' in writing or speech, which changes the meaning completely.
Pronouncing it 'SAIR-us' with the vowel of 'air'. Use the 'ee' vowel of 'seer'.

senses.definition: Long; polysyllabic.
senses.example: The most common use of "antidisestablishmentarianism" is as an example of a sesquipedalian word.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or given to the use of overly long words.
senses.example: Our dinner guest was so sesquipedalian that no one could understand what he said.

senses.definition: A long word.
senses.example: Her essay was full of sesquipedalians that made the simple argument hard to follow.

senses.definition: A person who uses long words.
senses.example: My old professor was a sesquipedalian who never said use when utilize sounded grander.

core.definition: Characterized by very long words; using or fond of long, polysyllabic words, often in a showy or pompous way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DAY, the fourth syllable. The 'qu' is pronounced 'kw', and the final syllables are quick and reduced, so the word ends with 'lee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or humorous. It usually mocks writing or speech that is showy and wordy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sesquipedalian mostly in writing, humor, or literary criticism, often to tease someone who picks needlessly big words. It is rarely used in ordinary conversation. Saying 'you're being sesquipedalian' can be a light joke among friends.

distinctions.note: Verbose means using too many words, while sesquipedalian means using long words, even if the sentence is short.
Pedantic describes an excessive concern with rules or details, while sesquipedalian focuses specifically on long vocabulary.

examples.everyday: My dad teases me for being sesquipedalian when I say 'unnecessarily complicated' instead of 'messy'.
examples.professional: Please avoid sesquipedalian jargon in the client summary; plain language will get the decision faster.
examples.analytical: Johnson's prose is often called sesquipedalian, yet its long words usually serve precision rather than mere display.

nuance.analogy: A sesquipedalian writer is like a tourist who carries a huge suitcase for a short trip, impressing people with the luggage rather than the journey.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sesquipedalis, meaning a foot and a half long, from sesqui- (one and a half) and pes (foot).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ses-kwi-PED-ah-lee-un', instead of the main stress on DAY.
Using it as a compliment for clear writing, when it usually means showy or excessively long words.

sesquipedalian.etymology: From *sesquipedal* + *-ian*, root from Latin *sēsquipedālis*, from Latin *sēsqui* (“one and a half times”) + Latin *pedālis* (“measuring a foot, foot”) (an adjective from *pēs* (“foot”)).

senses.definition: The cardinal sins enumerated by medieval philosophers and theologians: pride (or vanity, vainglory), envy, gluttony, greed (or avarice), lust, sloth (or acedia), and wrath (or anger).

core.definition: The seven vices of pride, envy, gluttony, greed, lust, sloth, and wrath, which medieval theologians taught were the roots of other sins.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SINS, with secondary stress on DEAD in deadly. In fast speech, seven becomes 'sev-n', and deadly often sounds like 'ded-lee' with a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names serious moral failings, though people often use it jokingly about treats or habits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the seven deadly sins in religious teaching, literature, and popular culture, and also jokingly about indulging, such as 'Ice cream is my favorite of the seven deadly sins.' In serious religious contexts, it is a traditional list rather than a formal doctrine. Saying 'the seven deadly sins' in conversation is usually playful, but it can sound heavy in a church setting.

distinctions.note: The Ten Commandments are a set of divine laws in Scripture, while the seven deadly sins are a later classification of vices and the motives behind wrongdoing.
Original sin refers to an inherited condition of human nature in Christian teaching, while the seven deadly sins are specific vices that people commit.

collocations: one of the seven deadly sins
commit one of the seven deadly sins
pride as the first of the seven deadly sins
sloth among the seven deadly sins
a medieval list of the seven deadly sins
the seven deadly sins and their virtues

examples.everyday: I just ate three slices of pizza, so I guess gluttony is one of my seven deadly sins today.
examples.professional: Half joking, our manager said skipping code review was pure sloth, one of the seven deadly sins.
examples.analytical: Medieval moralists such as Gregory the Great organized human vice into a short list, which Thomas Aquinas later analyzed in the Summa Theologiae.

nuance.analogy: Like the roots of a tree that feed many branches, the seven deadly sins are seen as the sources from which many other wrongdoings grow.
nuance.etymology: Deadly here means mortal or fatal to the soul, from Old English deadlic (deadly).
common_mistakes: Using deadly to mean sudden or dangerous in the physical sense; here it means mortal or spiritually fatal.
Saying 'seven cardinal sins' without knowing that cardinal here comes from Latin cardo (hinge or principle), meaning the chief sins, which is the Catholic term.
nuance.biblical_note: The list of seven deadly sins is not found in Scripture, but Proverbs 6:16-19 (RSV) describes seven things the LORD hates, which include haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and one who sows discord among brethren. Matthew 15:19 (RSV) lists evil thoughts, murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and slander as coming from the heart. The Greek word behind sin in these passages is hamartia (ἁμαρτία), meaning missing the mark.

traditions.view: Orthodox writers such as Evagrius Ponticus and John Cassian described eight evil thoughts (logismoi) that were later adapted into the seven-part scheme. The Orthodox tradition emphasizes ascetic struggle against the passions and does not treat a fixed list of seven as central.

The Catholic Church traditionally calls these the capital sins, from Latin caput (head), because they give rise to other sins. The Catechism discusses them in its treatment of sin, and confession addresses them as mortal or venial.

Most Protestants do not treat the list as formal doctrine, though they affirm the sins it names and use it in preaching and devotion. Lutheran and Reformed writers often emphasize sin as a turning away from God rather than a ranked list of vices.

seven-deadly-sins.etymology: From Middle English *dedly synnes sueyn*, *vij dedly synnes*.

core.definition: An ancient kingdom in southwestern Arabia, now Yemen, and its queen who visited King Solomon to test his wisdom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHEE. The second syllable is a weak uh, so do not stretch it into SHEE-bah.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a historical and religious name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often meet Sheba in Bible study, church history, or discussions of ancient trade. In everyday life it appears in phrases like the Queen of Sheba. The name is not used for a modern place in common speech.

distinctions.note: Seba is a different name in Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9, while Sheba in 1 Kings 10 refers to the kingdom and queen.

collocations: visit of the Queen of Sheba

examples.everyday: Our Sunday school class talked about the Queen of Sheba visiting Solomon.
examples.professional: In the lecture, I will explain how trade routes connected Sheba with the Mediterranean world.
examples.analytical: Matthew 12:42 calls her the queen of the South, presenting her as a witness who would rise up in judgment against a generation that rejected wisdom greater than Solomon's.

nuance.analogy: Sheba is like a legendary faraway kingdom in a story, known mainly through the visitor who traveled to meet a wise king.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Sheba, the name of a people and a region in southwestern Arabia, with uncertain original meaning.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Sheba as SHAY-ba; the American stress is on SHEE.
Confusing the Queen of Sheba with other queens in the Bible.
nuance.biblical_note: Sheba appears in Genesis 10:7 as a descendant of Cush, in 1 Kings 10:1-13 and 2 Chronicles 9:1-12 as the land whose queen visits Solomon, and in Matthew 12:42 as the queen of the South who will witness against the generation that rejects Jesus.

senses.definition: Emitting light.
Reflecting light.
Having a high polish or sheen.
senses.example: She polished the shining silver teapot until it reflected the kitchen light perfectly.

senses.definition: Having exceptional merit.
senses.example: a shining example

senses.definition: A bright emission of light; a gleam.
senses.example: In the dim attic, a faint shining caught my eye from the old brass key.

core.definition: Bright and glowing, either giving off light or reflecting it, and often used to praise someone's excellence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. End with the back nasal ng sound, and do not add a hard g. Spell it with one n, since shinning is a common misspelling.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests brightness, goodness or admirable excellence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shining both literally, as in shining stars, and figuratively, as in a shining example or a shining moment. The figurative sense is common in speeches, reviews and workplace praise. In casual talk, say bright for ordinary light and shiny for smooth surfaces.

distinctions.note: Shining describes light being given off or a bright, glowing quality, while shiny is simpler and refers to smooth reflective surfaces.
Bright is the general word for light or color, while shining adds a sense of glowing or polish and is often used figuratively.

examples.everyday: Her eyes were shining when she told us she had finally gotten the job.
examples.professional: Our Q3 team was a shining example of how to ship quality code under pressure.
examples.analytical: The shining light metaphor in Matthew's Gospel asks what the good works of the community reveal about God.

nuance.analogy: Like a freshly polished brass doorknob catching the morning light.
nuance.etymology: From shine (Old English scīnan) with the present participle ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Spelling it shinning with a double n
Using shining only literally, when it is also common for praising excellence
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew zāhar, to shine, appears in Daniel 12:3, where those who are wise are said to shine like the brightness of the sky. In Matthew 5:14, Jesus calls his followers the light of the world, an image of shining that points beyond the believer to God.

core.definition: The name of two men in the Bible: a son of Seir the Horite, and a son of Caleb in Judah's line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHOH. The second syllable is a reduced 'uhl', so say it as 'SHOH-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in genealogies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say this name outside Bible study and genealogy discussions. Because two different men share the name, say which Shobal you mean and give the verse.
