distinctions.note: Shimei and Shobal are different biblical names, and Shobal is used in genealogies while Shimei is a historical figure in the David narratives.

examples.everyday: When I read the family lists in Genesis, I always mix up Shobal with other names.
examples.professional: In my seminar, I separate the two men named Shobal by their genealogical lines.
examples.analytical: The double occurrence of the name Shobal in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 2 raises questions about the relation between Edomite and Judahite genealogies.

nuance.analogy: Shobal is like a common family name appearing in two different branches of a family tree.
common_mistakes: Assuming the two men named Shobal are the same person.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Shobal son of Seir the Horite is listed among the descendants of Seir in Genesis 36:20, and his sons appear in Genesis 36:23. A different Shobal, a son of Caleb, is named in 1 Chronicles 2:50 as the father of Kiriath-jearim.

senses.definition: The string or lace used to secure a shoe to the foot; a shoelace.
senses.example: Your shoestring is untied.

senses.definition: An object that is long and thin, like a shoestring (sense 1).
senses.example: shoestring French fries

senses.definition: A long, narrow cut of a food; a julienne.
senses.example: shoestring French fries

senses.definition: Chiefly in on a shoestring: very little money; a tight budget.
senses.example: He was able to organize the event on a shoestring.

senses.definition: To tackle (a player) using a shoestring tackle (“one made near the ground, close to a player's shoes”).
senses.example: The linebacker shoestringed the running back at the ankles and dropped him for a loss.

senses.definition: To catch (a ball) using a shoestring catch (“one made near the ground, close to a player's shoes”).
senses.example: The shortstop shoestringed the grounder and threw out the runner at first.

senses.definition: Of a catch or tackle: made near the ground, close to a player's shoes.
senses.example: The outfielder made a spectacular shoestring catch just above the grass.

core.definition: A very small budget, used in the phrase 'on a shoestring.' Also, a shoelace.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, shoe, with a long oo sound. The 'str' is one blended sound, and the final -ing is short i. Do not say 'shoo-STRING.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests very limited money, though the phrase can also suggest creativity or scrappy determination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on a shoestring' to describe doing something with a very small budget, as in 'run a business on a shoestring.' It is common in business, nonprofit, and sports contexts. In sports, a shoestring catch or tackle is a low, near-the-ground play, and fans use that term for a dramatic play.

distinctions.note: A tight budget is limited but workable, while a shoestring budget is extremely small and suggests doing everything with minimal money.
Frugal is a personal trait of careful spending, while on a shoestring describes the resources available to a project or organization.

examples.everyday: We threw the whole party together on a shoestring, so we borrowed folding chairs from the church.
examples.professional: The startup ran on a shoestring for two years before its first funding round, so every hire had to count.
examples.analytical: A theology of simplicity might recognize that living on a shoestring can be a discipline of trust rather than a sign of poverty.

nuance.analogy: A shoestring budget is like a thin rope holding up a big tent: it works, but there is almost no slack.
nuance.etymology: From shoe plus string, literally a lace for fastening a shoe.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in a shoestring' instead of 'on a shoestring.'
Using shoestring to mean a small object; it refers to a lace or a very small budget, not general size.

senses.definition: Too sweet to the point of disgust.
senses.example: The cheap wine was sickly sweet, and one glass was more than enough for me.

senses.definition: Highly sentimental.

core.definition: Too sweet in a way that becomes unpleasant, or overly sentimental and insincere in tone.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on sweet, while sickly has lighter secondary stress. Link the words smoothly so it sounds like 'sik-lee-SWEET.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes food as too sweet and people or speech as fake, overly sugary, or sentimental.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sickly sweet for desserts, drinks, or candy that taste too sugary, and also for a smile, voice, or message that seems fake or cloying. It is a common, casual phrase, and calling someone's manner sickly sweet can be an insult. When speaking politely about food at a restaurant, you may prefer 'very sweet' to avoid sounding rude.

distinctions.note: Sugary describes sweetness neutrally; sickly sweet describes sweetness that has become unpleasant.
Saccharine is more formal and focuses on excessive sentimentality; sickly sweet is more casual and can describe taste or manner.
Cloying means too much and tiring; sickly sweet adds a sense of disgust or fakeness.

examples.everyday: This lemonade is sickly sweet, so can I get a little water?
examples.professional: His sickly sweet emails about the deadline did not hide the fact that the project was behind.
examples.analytical: The poem's sickly sweet sentiment collapses under its own sentimentality, failing to convey any real grief.

nuance.analogy: Like a candy so heavy with sugar that one bite is enough, the sweetness becomes a problem instead of a pleasure.
nuance.etymology: Sickly comes from Old English seoclic, sick; sweet from Old English swete, pleasant to taste.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sick sweet' without the -ly in sickly, which is not standard.
Using sickly sweet to praise something positively, when it almost always sounds negative.

senses.definition: A position that requires little to no work, or easy work, but still gives an ample payment; a cushy job.
(historical) An ecclesiastical benefice without the care of souls.
senses.example: The priest held a sinecure that paid him handsomely without requiring him to tend any parishioners.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Requiring no work for an ample reward.
senses.example: The consulting job was a sinecure, with a generous salary and almost no real responsibilities.

senses.definition: Having the appearance of functionality without being of any actual use or purpose.
senses.example: The committee was a sinecure, meeting monthly to approve decisions already made elsewhere.

senses.definition: To put or place in a sinecure.
senses.example: The board sinecured its retiring director with a title and an office but no duties.

core.definition: A job or position that requires little or no work but pays well; a cushy job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced 'ih' rather than 'ee' or 'eh'. Keep the r in the final syllable, which is pronounced 'kyoor' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly disapproving; it implies unearned pay and suggests the job is a privilege rather than real work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sinecure mainly in journalism, politics, and business writing when they want to criticize a job that pays for little work. In casual conversation people more often say 'cushy job' or 'easy gig'. Using it can sound a bit stiff, but it is a precise word to know.

distinctions.note: A cushy job is casual slang for an easy, comfortable job, while sinecure is more formal and often implies a position created or held for patronage or with no real duties.
A sideline is a secondary job done alongside a main one, not an easy job with pay for doing nothing.

examples.everyday: My cousin got a sinecure at the county office, and he just shows up to sign a few papers.
examples.professional: The advisory board seat is basically a sinecure, since nobody expects him to attend the meetings.
examples.analytical: Some medieval church offices became sinecures that paid clergy who never served the parish.

nuance.analogy: A sinecure is like a gym membership you pay for every month but never use, except the money comes to you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sine cura, 'without care', originally a church office with income but no pastoral duties.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'sin' like the moral term; it is 'SY' as in 'sigh'.
Using sinecure to mean any job that is simply enjoyable rather than one that pays for little work.

sinecure.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin *sine cūrā*, formed from Medieval Latin *sine* (“without”) + *cūrā* (“care, charge, cure”).

senses.definition: One who sips.
senses.example: My grandmother was a patient sipper who nursed one cup of tea all afternoon.

senses.definition: A glass with a narrow tube on one side, for sipping port, etc.
A drinking straw.
One who sips lean, a poly-substance drink used as a recreational drug.
senses.example: Friends said he had become a heavy sipper of lean, mixing codeine syrup into soda every night.

core.definition: A drinking straw, or a small glass or cup with a narrow tube used for sipping a drink slowly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, SIP. The final -er is a weak, r-colored schwa, not a strong 'ur' sound, so it is two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an object and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sipper mostly for a glass with a built-in straw or a special cup for drinking slowly, such as at a bar or restaurant offering wine or whiskey tastings. The more common everyday word for a bendy tube is straw. The sense of a person who sips is rare in American speech.

distinctions.note: A straw is any thin tube for drinking; a sipper is usually a glass or cup with a narrow tube built in.
A sippy cup is a spill-proof cup for toddlers, while a sipper is used by adults for slow drinking.

examples.everyday: Grab a sipper for the iced tea so it doesn't spill in the car.
examples.professional: The wine tasting flight comes with a sipper glass so guests can taste without spilling.
examples.analytical: A sipper limits the flow, so the drinker controls how much liquid reaches the palate, which changes how the aroma and flavor are perceived.

nuance.analogy: A sipper is like a tiny dam that lets only a small stream of drink reach your mouth at a time.
nuance.etymology: From sip plus -er, 'one that does something'.
common_mistakes: Saying SIP-er with a strong final 'ur' sound instead of a weak schwa.
Using sipper for a regular straw in everyday talk; Americans say straw for most cases.

senses.definition: Skirting boards collectively.
senses.example: The contractor installed new white skirting throughout the living room and both bedrooms.

senses.definition: Skirts collectively; material for skirts.
senses.example: The fabric store had a wide selection of skirting in cotton, linen, and wool blends.

senses.definition: The act of one who skirts around something, or avoids it.

core.definition: The act of avoiding a difficult topic or obstacle by going around it, as in skirting the issue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ir is r-colored, and the t is crisp in careful speech but often becomes a quick flap in casual American speech, sounding close to SKUR-ding.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, since it implies evasion. 'Skirting the issue' is mildly critical, while physically skirting an area is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mostly in phrases like 'the skirting of the issue,' but the verb is far more common: 'She skirted the question.' The sense of a strip along a wall is mainly British and is called a baseboard in the US. The sense of fabric for skirts is rare today.

distinctions.note: Evasion is a broader term for avoiding a question or duty, often dishonestly; skirting is about going around a topic without touching it directly.
Dodging suggests quick, sudden avoidance, while skirting suggests staying near the subject without facing it.

examples.everyday: He kept skirting the question about when he would be home, so I knew something was wrong.
examples.professional: The project update skirted the real delays, so the team never discussed the risks.
examples.analytical: Her essay repeatedly skirts the central objection, offering examples in place of argument.

nuance.analogy: Like walking around the edge of a puddle without stepping in it, skirting avoids the hard middle of a topic.
nuance.etymology: From the verb skirt, from Old Norse skyrta (a shirt or tunic); the sense of going along an edge developed later.
common_mistakes: Using skirting for the American baseboard; in the US, ask for baseboard.
Writing skirt on the issue with a wrong preposition; say skirt the issue or skirt around the issue.

senses.definition: In a skittish manner.

core.definition: In a nervous, easily startled way, as if afraid of a sudden movement or surprise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ish is short and unstressed, and the final -ly is a light lee sound, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it suggests nervousness and can describe animals or people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use skittishly mainly in writing, especially in descriptions of horses, cats, or nervous people, or in business news about markets. In speech, nervously or jumpy is more common. The adjective skittish is far more common: 'The horse was skittish.'

distinctions.note: Nervously is the general word for anxiety; skittishly suggests quick, jumpy reactions, like an animal startled by a sound.
Warily means cautiously and deliberately; skittishly suggests more sudden, easily startled behavior.

examples.everyday: The new puppy looked at me skittishly and backed under the table.
examples.professional: Investors reacted skittishly to the announcement, selling before the details came out.
examples.analytical: The author writes skittishly about her own conclusions, qualifying each claim before it can be tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a deer that flinches at a twig snapping, the response moves before the threat is clear.
nuance.etymology: From skittish plus the adverb suffix -ly; skittish is of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using skittishly for a calm person; it means jumpy or nervous.
Pronouncing the first vowel long, as in SKY-tish; it is a short i.

senses.definition: Both untrue and harmful to a reputation.

core.definition: Containing false statements that are harmful to someone's reputation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable is 'rus', not 'ross'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies that a statement is both false and damaging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'slanderous' in legal, journalistic, and formal writing, and sometimes in everyday talk to describe a rumor or post. It means something false and harmful, so do not use it just to mean rude or unkind. In a dispute, a lawyer might say 'that statement is slanderous'.

distinctions.note: 'Defamatory' is the formal legal term; 'slanderous' is more common in everyday American English.
A critical statement may be harsh but true or fair; a slanderous one must be false and harmful.

examples.everyday: That post about my dad is slanderous, and I want it taken down.
examples.professional: Legal flagged the memo because two of its claims about the contractor are slanderous.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the pamphlet's slanderous charges depend more on innuendo than on evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a false label stuck to a jar: it misrepresents what is inside and damages its value.
nuance.etymology: From slander, with the adjective suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Using 'slanderous' for anything unpleasant, when it requires both falsehood and harm.
Confusing it with 'slanderer', which is the person rather than the statement.

senses.definition: A pill or tablet having a soporific effect.
senses.example: The doctor prescribed a sleeping pill for the jet lag, but it left me groggy all morning.

core.definition: A pill that makes a person sleep or helps them fall asleep.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PILL, and the first word has a lighter stress. In fast speech sleeping often sounds like sleepin.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical talk. People may worry about dependence, so they often talk about taking something to sleep instead of naming a pill.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sleeping pill or sleep aid; sleep aid is broader and includes melatonin and other products. Doctors usually prescribe sleeping pills for short periods because of dependence risks. Over-the-counter options include diphenhydramine, sold as Benadryl, and melatonin, and people often say I take melatonin to sleep.

distinctions.note: Sleeping tablet is mainly British; Americans say sleeping pill.
Sleep aid is broader and includes melatonin and natural remedies, while sleeping pill usually means a drug.
Sedative is a medical term for a drug that calms or induces sleep; sleeping pill is everyday language for a sleep-inducing drug.

examples.everyday: I haven't slept in days, so my doctor gave me a sleeping pill.
examples.professional: The pharmacy team reminded patients that a sleeping pill should never be combined with alcohol.
examples.analytical: Sleeping pills can relieve the symptoms of insomnia, but they do not address the underlying causes of disturbed rest.

nuance.analogy: A sleeping pill works like a dimmer switch for the brain, turning down alertness so sleep can arrive.
nuance.etymology: Sleeping from sleep; pill from Latin pilula, little ball.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally; the main stress belongs on PILL.
Saying sleeping tablet in an American pharmacy; sleeping pill is the normal term.

senses.definition: A noxious mixture of particulates and gases that is the result of urban air pollution.
senses.example: Los Angeles smog hung over the freeway on the hot August afternoon.

senses.definition: To get a smog check; to check a vehicle or have it checked for emissions.
senses.example: If the car is more than five years old, you'll have to have it smogged before you can register it.

core.definition: Dirty, hazy air caused by vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and sunlight reacting with pollutants over a city.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the open 'ah' of 'cot', which many Americans share with 'caught', so keep it short and open. End with a clear hard 'g' and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unhealthy, unpleasant air and is linked to health warnings and environmental concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'smog' in everyday talk about weather and air quality, as in 'The smog is terrible today' or 'There's an air quality alert because of smog.' In California and some other states, 'smog check' is a routine vehicle emissions inspection, and people say they need to 'get smogged' in that sense. Outside those contexts, use 'air pollution' in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Fog is a natural cloud of water droplets close to the ground, while smog is a pollution haze produced by human activity.
Haze is a general term for reduced visibility from dust, heat or moisture, while smog specifically means pollution from urban activity.
Pollution is the broad term for any contamination of air, water or land, while smog is one specific kind of air pollution.

examples.everyday: The smog is so thick today that I can hardly see the mountains from my apartment.
examples.professional: The air quality team issued a smog alert, so we moved the outdoor event to next week.
examples.analytical: Smog is a visible sign of an economic system that externalizes its costs onto the public.

nuance.analogy: Smog is like a dirty curtain hanging over a city: it blocks the view and makes every breath feel heavier.
nuance.etymology: A blend of 'smoke' and 'fog', coined in the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using 'smog' for ordinary smoke from a campfire or a single fire, when 'smoke' is the better word.
Confusing 'smog' with 'fog' and calling a natural morning mist 'smog'.

senses.definition: A certain number (multiple but not all).
senses.example: Some enjoy spicy food, others prefer it milder.

senses.definition: An indefinite quantity.
senses.example: Can I have some of them?

senses.definition: An indefinite amount; a part. Used mostly with abstract and nonliving objects.
senses.example: Please give me some of the cake.

senses.definition: A nonzero, unspecified proportion of (a bounded set of countable things): at least two.
senses.example: Some people like camping.

senses.definition: A nonzero, unspecified quantity or number of (an unbounded set of countable things).
senses.example: Would you like some grapes?

senses.definition: An unspecified amount of (something uncountable).
senses.example: Would you like some water?

senses.definition: A certain, an unspecified or unknown.
senses.example: I've just met some guy who said he knew you.

senses.definition: A considerable quantity or number of.
senses.example: He had edited the paper for some years.

senses.definition: Approximately, about (with a number).
senses.example: She has worked at the company for some thirty years now. (31 and two months, to be exact.)

senses.definition: Emphasizing a number.
senses.example: She has worked at the company for some five years now! How remarkable!

senses.definition: A remarkable.
senses.example: He is some acrobat!

senses.definition: Of a measurement: approximately, roughly.
senses.example: I guess he must have weighed some 90 kilos.

senses.definition: Somewhat, a little.
senses.example: I felt some better after the nap, though my head still ached.

core.definition: An unspecified amount or number of something; a certain quantity or a few of a group, not all of it.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single stressed syllable, pronounced the same as 'sum'. In unstressed speech it reduces to 'suhm', so 'some of them' sounds like 'suhm uv them'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'some' in positive statements and offers ('I'd like some water'), while 'any' is used in negatives and questions ('Do you have any water?'). As an adverb, 'some' with a number ('some 200 people') is common in American news and speech, but 'somewhat' is preferred in formal writing for degree.

distinctions.note: 'Some' is used mainly in affirmative sentences and offers, while 'any' is used in negatives, questions, and conditionals.
'Several' means a specific number greater than two but not many, while 'some' is vague about the number.
'A few' means a small number of countable things, and it is often more positive in tone, while 'some' can refer to a larger or unclear amount.

examples.everyday: Can I get some more coffee, please?
examples.professional: We still need some clarification on the Q3 numbers before we send the report to finance.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that grace precedes human choice, while others stress the cooperation of the will.

nuance.analogy: 'Some' is like a scoop taken from a larger pile: you get part of it, but not all of it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'sum', meaning 'a certain one' or 'a certain amount'.
common_mistakes: Using 'some' in negative sentences, such as 'I don't have some money'; say 'I don't have any money'.
Confusing the pronunciation with 'sum' in a way that changes meaning in fast speech; the two sound the same, so context matters.

some.etymology: From Middle English *som*, *sum*, from Old English *sum* (“some, a certain one”), from **sum*, from Proto-Germanic **sumaz* (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-Indo-European **sem-* (“one, whole”).

senses.definition: Resembling a song.
senses.example: a songlike adagio

core.definition: Resembling a song, especially in melody, rhythm, or smooth, flowing sound.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on the -like ending. The final syllable has the diphthong 'ai', as in 'bike'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises a voice, poem, or prose for its musical quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use songlike mostly in describing voices, poems, or writing with a melodic rhythm, often in reviews or criticism. It is not a casual word for everyday conversation. In speech, people more often say 'like a song' or 'melodic'.

distinctions.note: Melodic means having a pleasant tune, while songlike suggests the quality of singing or song-like phrasing even without a tune.
Lyrical describes expressive, poetic language or feeling, while songlike focuses on sound and rhythm.

examples.professional: The presenter's songlike cadence made the keynote easy to follow, though the slides were dense.
examples.analytical: Whitman's long lines often read as songlike, even though they are not set to music.

nuance.analogy: Like a melody that stays in your head after the music stops.
nuance.etymology: From song (from Old English sang) plus -like (from Old English -lic).
common_mistakes: Writing 'song like' as two words in formal writing, where songlike is the standard form.
Using songlike as a noun, when it is only an adjective.

senses.definition: Unhappiness, woe.
An instance or cause of unhappiness.
senses.example: Parting is such sweet sorrow.

senses.definition: To feel or express grief.
To feel grief over; to mourn, regret.

core.definition: A deep feeling of sadness caused by loss, disappointment, or suffering; grief.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make it sound like sar, with the r pronounced clearly. Many Americans use the same vowel as in cot and car, so sorrow rhymes with barrow.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious, heavy sadness, often connected with loss or moral pain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sorrow in serious or emotional contexts: a funeral, a condolence card, a sermon, or a moving story. In everyday talk people more often say sad, upset, or heartbroken. Sorrow sounds slightly literary when used casually, so a natural spoken choice is I'm so sorry for your loss.

distinctions.note: Grief is the sharp, often prolonged response to a death or major loss, while sorrow is a broader feeling of sadness that may be less intense.
Sadness is the everyday word for feeling unhappy, while sorrow is deeper, more serious, and more formal.

examples.everyday: I was filled with sorrow when I heard that your dad had passed away.
examples.professional: The team shared its sorrow after the outage, but the immediate priority was restoring service for customers.
examples.analytical: Ecclesiastes presents sorrow not as an accident of life but as a condition that wisdom must learn to face honestly.

nuance.analogy: Sorrow is like a heavy coat on a cold day: it weighs on you slowly and steadily, and you can carry it for a long time.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sorg or sorh, 'grief, anxiety', of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Using sorrow for a small disappointment, as in 'I felt sorrow when my coffee was cold'; use disappointed instead.
Confusing sorrow with sorry, which is an apology or a mild feeling of regret.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, sorrow usually translates 'etsev' (עֶצֶב), meaning pain, toil, or grief, and in Greek it often translates 'lupe' (λύπη), meaning grief or distress. Genesis 3:16-17 links pain and toil with the consequences of the fall. Isaiah 53:3 calls the Servant a man of sorrows, and 2 Corinthians 7:10 contrasts godly grief, which leads to repentance, with worldly grief, which leads to death.

senses.definition: A technology that handles access to computer files containing source code so that several users can work on the files without interfering with each other's changes.
Measures applied to potentially-infected people that reduce their chances of infecting others.
senses.example: Source control measures, such as masks for people with symptoms, reduced transmission in the clinic.

senses.definition: Measures applied to the source of an infection to reduce further contamination and spread.
senses.example: Health officials pursued source control by closing the contaminated well and disinfecting the water main.

core.definition: A system that tracks changes to source code files so several developers can edit the same project without overwriting each other's work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOURCE, and the r in both words is clearly pronounced in General American. Say the t in control as a flap, like a soft d, so it sounds like kun-TROHL.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Developers use this term in everyday engineering talk, meetings and job postings. It usually refers to tools such as Git, and people often say version control as a near-synonym. In infection-related contexts, the phrase has an unrelated meaning, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Version control is the broader term for tracking file history; source control is often used for the same systems when the files are code.
Source code is the text of the program itself; source control is the system that manages changes to that code.

examples.everyday: My buddy who works in software said their team uses source control so nobody messes up each other's code.
examples.professional: Please make sure every change goes through source control before the release branch is cut.
examples.analytical: Source control makes the history of a codebase auditable, since each change is recorded with its author and reason.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared document with a complete edit history, where you can see who changed what and undo any change.
nuance.etymology: Source comes from Latin surgere via Old French source, meaning a spring or origin; control comes from Medieval Latin contrarotulus, a duplicate register.
common_mistakes: Saying 'source control' for infection control in a software conversation, which causes confusion.
Stressing control on the second word as in a verb phrase; the phrase is stressed on SOURCE.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being sovereign.
senses.example: The king's sovereignty was absolute, and no nobleman dared challenge his decrees.

senses.definition: Of a ruler (especially a monarch): supreme authority or dominion over something.
Of a nation or other polity: the state of being able to control resources, make laws independently, and otherwise govern itself without the coercion or concurrence of other polities.
senses.example: The treaty recognized the country's sovereignty over its coastal waters and natural resources.

senses.definition: Of a person: the liberty to decide one's actions and thoughts.
senses.example: Many people value personal sovereignty over their bodies, choices, and daily routines.

senses.definition: Pre-eminent or superior excellence; also, superior ability to achieve something; mastery.
senses.example: He demonstrated sovereignty over the difficult material, answering every question without hesitation.

senses.definition: A territory under the rule of a sovereign; an independent or self-governing nation or other polity.
senses.example: The island remained under Dutch sovereignty until the nineteenth century.

core.definition: The supreme authority of a state or ruler to govern itself and make its own laws.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllables reduce quickly. Keep the r clear and end with a light 'tee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sovereignty in political news, law, and philosophy, often in phrases about a nation's rights. In theology, it refers to God's supreme rule over creation. In casual talk, people more often say 'control' or 'independence.' Political debates about sovereignty can be emotionally charged.

distinctions.note: Independence means not being ruled by others; sovereignty adds the legal authority to make and enforce laws.
Authority is any power to command; sovereignty is the highest, final power within a state or over oneself.

examples.everyday: A lot of people here are upset that the treaty might cut into our national sovereignty.
examples.professional: Legal said the new data-sharing agreement doesn't affect our sovereignty over the stored records.
examples.analytical: Calvin's doctrine of divine sovereignty grounds God's rule in his freedom rather than in human merit.

nuance.analogy: Like the final say in a family about what happens in the home, though on a national scale.
nuance.etymology: From Old French soverainete, from soverain (supreme), from Medieval Latin superanus.
common_mistakes: Using sovereignty for everyday personal independence, which sounds too formal.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.

sovereignty.etymology: From Late Middle English *sovereynte*, *souvereynte*, from Anglo-Norman *sovereyneté*, *soverentee*, and Old French *soveraineté*, *souveraineté*, from *soverain* + *-té*.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being spacious.
senses.example: The apartment's spaciousness made the cramped rooms of our old house seem tiny.

core.definition: The quality of having plenty of room, so that a place feels open and not crowded.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SPAY. The final '-ness' is a reduced schwa, /nəs/, not 'nes' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment about a home, car or venue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spaciousness' in real-estate listings, design talk and reviews, as in 'the spaciousness of the kitchen'. In everyday talk, people more often say 'room' or 'roominess'. It is usually said with admiration.

distinctions.note: Roominess is more everyday and informal, while spaciousness is more formal and polished.
Size is a measurement, while spaciousness describes how room feels when you use it.
Openness can mean lack of barriers or frank attitude, while spaciousness is specifically about room.

examples.everyday: I love the spaciousness of this apartment; there's room for a real dining table.
examples.professional: The renovation prioritizes spaciousness in the lobby, which helps with foot traffic during events.
examples.analytical: The poet's spaciousness of imagery gives the reader room to think without rushing toward a conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a good conversation with room for silence, the spaciousness lets ideas breathe.
nuance.etymology: From spacious, from Latin spatiosus, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'spacious' as 'spay-shuss' with a hard s; the middle syllable is a soft 'shus'.
Using 'spaciousness' for crowded places, which is the opposite meaning.

senses.definition: A tree structure which includes all vertices of a graph.

core.definition: In graph theory, a subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex of the original graph.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on tree and secondary on span. The -ing is short and unstressed, so say it quickly as a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in computer science and mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: Computer scientists and network engineers use spanning tree when designing networks without loops, such as the Spanning Tree Protocol in Ethernet switches. In graph theory courses, spanning trees are central to algorithms like Kruskal's and Prim's. Americans say it as a fixed compound noun.

distinctions.note: A minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total edge weight is as small as possible, while any spanning tree need not be minimal.

collocations: find a spanning tree of the graph

examples.everyday: My network admin said the office switches use a spanning tree to avoid loops.
examples.professional: We can use a spanning tree to connect all the nodes in the sensor network with the fewest links.
examples.analytical: A spanning tree of a connected graph G is a subgraph that contains every vertex of G and is acyclic and connected.

nuance.analogy: A spanning tree is like the skeleton of a road map: it connects every town using just enough roads and no loops.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on span, which blurs the compound; keep the main stress on tree.
Forgetting that the tree must include every vertex, not just some of them.

senses.definition: To place under the influence of a magical spell; to enchant or bewitch with a spell.
To captivate, or hold the attention of, as if by a magic spell; to entrance.

core.definition: To hold someone's complete attention so that they are fascinated or unable to look away.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, spell, and the final syllable bind rhymes with 'mind' and ends in a clear d. Do not stress the second syllable, as in spell-BIND.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting that someone is captivating, though it can imply losing control of one's attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spellbind mostly in writing, reviews and speeches to praise a performer, book or speaker. In everyday talk, people more often say 'captivating' or 'really gripping.' The adjective spellbinding is much more common than the verb in American speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Fascinate is a general word for holding interest, while spellbind suggests a stronger, almost magical hold.
Enthrall is close in strength but more literary, while spellbind is more common in reviews and descriptions of speakers.
Captivate is broader and more common in everyday talk, while spellbind emphasizes a total hold on attention.

examples.everyday: The storyteller at the campfire spellbound the kids, and nobody wanted to go to bed.
examples.professional: Her keynote on data ethics spellbound the room, although the audience had not yet seen the evidence.
examples.analytical: Good rhetoric can spellbind an audience even when its argument does not survive careful scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: To spellbind is to tie someone's attention with an invisible rope, so they cannot look away from the performance.
nuance.etymology: From spell, meaning a magical formula or charm, plus bind, from Old English bindan; the verb developed in the sense of enchanting through the influence of a spell.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in spell-BIND, which sounds like a different word.
Using spellbind as a casual synonym for interesting, when it suggests a stronger, almost total hold on attention.

senses.definition: To reveal a secret; to disclose information.
senses.example: They had planned it as a surprise party, but somebody spilled the beans.

core.definition: To reveal a secret or share information that was supposed to be kept hidden.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the word 'beans'. In casual speech, 'the' becomes a quick schwa, and the phrase links together so it sounds like 'spil-thuh-BEENZ'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests someone broke a confidence, sometimes by accident.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this phrase when someone reveals a surprise, such as a party or a gift. A natural reply is 'Oh no, who spilled the beans?' or 'I didn't mean to spill the beans!' It is informal, so avoid it in formal writing or serious business talk.

distinctions.vs: let the cat out of the bag
distinctions.note: Both mean revealing a secret, but 'let the cat out of the bag' often refers to a secret that is revealed by mistake.
'Tell' is a neutral word for sharing information, while 'spill the beans' suggests revealing something that should have stayed hidden.

examples.everyday: Okay, who spilled the beans about the surprise party? Mom already knows.
examples.professional: Please don't spill the beans about the reorganization before the director announces it at the all-hands meeting.
examples.analytical: The scene turns on a character who, unable to keep silence, spills the beans and exposes the conspiracy to the crowd.

nuance.analogy: A secret is like a bag of beans: it is fine as long as it stays closed, but once it spills, everyone can see what is inside.
nuance.etymology: The origin is uncertain, though many believe it comes from an old American expression, possibly from a bean-counting or bean-sorting game.
common_mistakes: Saying 'spill beans' without 'the'.
Using it for literal spilling of beans in a formal report where a neutral verb would be better.

synonyms: let the cat out of the bag
spill-the-beans.etymology: First attested in 20th century American English.

conversation.text: Come on, spill the beans. How did the date go?
Who spilled the beans about the reorganization?
Don't spill the beans to Mom about the surprise party.

inflections: spilled the beans, spilt the beans

senses.definition: Spit, usually frothy and of a milky coloration.
senses.example: The old dog's mouth was flecked with white spittle after it finished barking.

senses.definition: Something frothy and white that resembles spit.
Spit-up or drool of an infant.
A small sort of spade.
senses.example: The gardener reached for the spittle to loosen the soil around the roots.

senses.definition: To dig or stir with a small spade.
senses.example: Before planting the tulips, she spittled the flower bed to loosen the hard clay.

core.definition: Saliva, especially when it is foamy or spat out, or the frothy spit of an infant or drooling person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The tt is pronounced as a single t, and the last syllable is a light, reduced 'uhl'; do not insert a vowel between the t and the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to unpleasant; it describes saliva in a way that can sound graphic or old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use spittle in everyday conversation; they say spit or saliva. The word sounds literary, biblical or medical, so it can seem old-fashioned in casual speech. You will mostly see it in writing, in medical contexts and in Bible reading.

distinctions.note: Saliva is the neutral term for the liquid in the mouth; spittle is saliva that has been expelled or looks foamy.
Drool is saliva running out of the mouth; spittle is saliva that is spat out or frothing.
Phlegm is mucus from the airways and throat; spittle is saliva.

examples.everyday: When the kid yelled at the game, spittle flew everywhere.
examples.professional: The nurse wiped spittle from the infant's chin before writing her feeding notes.
examples.analytical: Mark's gospel describes Jesus using spittle in healing, joining a physical act to a word of power.

nuance.analogy: Spittle is like the foam on a shaken soda: the same liquid, but agitated into something frothy.
nuance.etymology: From Old English spætl, related to spit.
common_mistakes: Using spittle as an everyday word; in conversation, say saliva or spit.
Pronouncing the last syllable with a full vowel, as in 'spit-tul'; it is a light, reduced 'uhl'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is ptysma (spittle). In Mark 8:23 Jesus uses spittle on a blind man's eyes as part of his healing. In John 9:6 he makes clay from spittle and applies it to a blind man's eyes. In Mark 7:33 he spits and touches a deaf man's tongue, a healing gesture using ordinary bodily means.

spittle.etymology: Alteration of dialectal *spattle* (by association with *spit*), from Old English *spātl*, which is related to *spǣtan* (whence *spit*).

senses.definition: A fit of immoderate laughter or merriment.
senses.example: Grandpa's terrible pun sent the kids into a spleen of helpless laughter.

senses.definition: In vertebrates, including humans, a ductless vascular gland, located in the upper left abdomen near the stomach, which destroys old red blood cells, removes debris from the bloodstream, acts as a reservoir of blood, and produces lymphocytes.
senses.example: The doctor said the ultrasound showed his spleen was slightly enlarged.

senses.definition: To annoy or irritate.
senses.example: Her endless chatter about the meeting began to spleen everyone in the room.

senses.definition: To complain; to rail; to vent one's spleen.
senses.example: He spleened about the unfair schedule for twenty minutes at the bar.

senses.definition: To remove the spleen, or, by extension, to gore.
senses.example: The surgeons decided to spleen the patient after the car crash ruptured the organ.

senses.definition: To excise or remove.
senses.example: The editor spleened three paragraphs from the essay to tighten the argument.

core.definition: Bitter anger or irritation, usually expressed as a complaint, mainly in the phrase 'vent one's spleen'.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long ee vowel, as in 'green', with the s, p and l at the start. Do not use the short i of 'spin' or 'splint'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes bitter, explosive anger, and the phrase often sounds dramatic or old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: The anatomical organ is the most common sense in medicine, but in everyday talk Americans rarely use spleen for anger. The idiom 'vent one's spleen' appears mainly in literature, journalism and formal writing. In conversation, Americans say 'let off steam', 'rant' or 'vent', so those are the natural choices for everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Anger is the general word for the feeling, while spleen is a literary term for a bitter, venting kind of anger.
Splenic is an adjective meaning relating to the spleen organ, and it has nothing to do with temper.

examples.everyday: Mom finally vented her spleen about the landlord, and everyone at the table went quiet.
examples.professional: The manager vented his spleen about the late deliveries in the meeting, though nobody could fix them that day.
examples.analytical: Swift vented his spleen against the stupidity of public life, and his satire gains force from that anger.

nuance.analogy: Like a pressure cooker: the anger builds up and then bursts out in a rant.
nuance.etymology: From Latin splen, from Greek splēn; the anger sense comes from the old belief that the spleen caused moods.
common_mistakes: Using spleen for everyday anger in casual speech, where 'vent' or 'rant' sounds more natural.
Confusing spleen with splenetic, which is the adjective for irritable.

spleen.etymology: From Middle English *splene*, *splen*, from Anglo-Norman *espleen* and Old French *esplein*, *esplen*, from Latin *splēn* (“milt”), from Ancient Greek *σπλήν* (“the spleen”).

senses.definition: Possessing or displaying splendor; shining; very bright.
senses.example: a splendid sun

senses.definition: Gorgeous; magnificent; sumptuous; of remarkable beauty, especially of an elaborate or luxurious kind.
senses.example: a splendid palace

senses.definition: Brilliant, excellent, of a very high standard.
senses.example: We had a splendid view of the harbor from our hotel room on the top floor.

core.definition: Excellent, wonderful, or very good; often used to express approval or agreement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is short and quick, so the word has two clear beats, SPLEN-did, not three.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Splendid can sound a little old-fashioned or formal in casual American speech, so it may seem polite, warm or slightly stiff depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say splendid mostly in polite or older speech, as in That sounds splendid. In everyday talk, great, wonderful, or awesome are more common. The sense of magnificent beauty is more literary.

distinctions.note: Great is the everyday American choice; splendid is more formal and suggests a higher level of excellence.
Magnificent emphasizes impressive grandeur or size, while splendid often praises something pleasant and admirable.

examples.everyday: Dinner tonight at seven sounds splendid, thanks for suggesting it.
examples.professional: That's splendid work on the migration plan, and the client will be very pleased.
examples.analytical: The argument is splendid in its structure, though its premises deserve closer scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like a fine dress or a bright sunrise, it shows something that impresses you at first glance.
nuance.etymology: From Latin splendidus, meaning shining or brilliant, from splendere, to shine.
common_mistakes: Using splendid as a casual default for good in everyday speech, which can sound stiff.
Stressing the second syllable, as in splen-DID.

senses.definition: To dress or arrange smartly, elegantly, and neatly; to smarten.
senses.example: We should spruce up the living room before the guests arrive Saturday.

senses.definition: To refresh, revamp; to freshen or improve something, especially its appearance.
senses.example: Fresh paint and some new curtains would do a lot to spruce up this dark room.

core.definition: To make something or someone look neater, smarter, or more attractive, often by cleaning, tidying, or refreshing it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, and spruce is pronounced sproos, with the vowel of 'Lou' rather than 'spruice'. In speech it links smoothly, so 'spruce it up' sounds like 'sproo-si-TUP'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a pleasant improvement in appearance, often with a small amount of effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spruce up for tidying a room before guests arrive, dressing up for an event, or giving an old place a fresh look. You can say 'Let's spruce up the place' or 'You should spruce up a little before the interview.' A natural reply is 'Good idea, I'll do that' or simply 'Thanks for the tip.'

distinctions.note: Clean up focuses on removing dirt or mess, while spruce up focuses on making something look more attractive or stylish.
Renovate means to rebuild or repair substantially, whereas spruce up is a lighter, cosmetic improvement.

examples.everyday: We have guests coming tonight, so I'm going to spruce up the living room a little.
examples.professional: Let's spruce up the onboarding deck a bit before we send it to the client on Friday.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that many reform efforts merely spruce up an institution's public image without changing its underlying structure.

nuance.analogy: Like putting fresh paint and new curtains in an old house: the foundation stays the same, but the place looks much better.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb built on spruce (adjective meaning neat and smart), probably from Middle English spruce, meaning Prussian.
common_mistakes: Using spruce up only for dirty things; it means making something look better, not just cleaner.
Pronouncing spruce with a short u or a final -ce sound; the vowel is long oo and the ending is -s.

senses.definition: To reject disdainfully; contemn; scorn.
To reject something by pushing it away with the foot.
senses.example: He spurned the rolling can with his boot, sending it clattering down the alley.

senses.definition: To waste; fail to make the most of (an opportunity)
senses.example: They spurned a golden opportunity to expand the business during the boom years.

senses.definition: An act of spurning; a scornful rejection.
senses.example: Her spurn of the offer stung him more than he expected.

senses.definition: A body of coal left to sustain an overhanging mass.
senses.example: Miners left a spurn of coal to hold up the roof above the tunnel.

core.definition: To reject someone or something with scorn or contempt, refusing an offer or affection in a harsh way.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the American r-colored vowel, like 'urn' or 'burn.' Keep the r clear and do not add a separate vowel before the n.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a harsh, proud, or insulting refusal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spurn' mostly in writing, storytelling, or formal speech, often about rejecting an offer of love or friendship. In everyday conversation, people more often say 'turn down' or 'reject.' Saying 'she spurned his proposal' sounds dramatic and literary.

distinctions.note: Reject is neutral and common, while spurn adds a sense of scorn or disdain.
Decline is polite and formal, while spurn is harsh and contemptuous.

examples.everyday: I offered to help her move, but she spurned me and said she would manage alone.
examples.professional: The board spurned the vendor's proposal outright, without even reviewing the pricing.
examples.analytical: The prophet describes a people who spurned the covenant, treating God's mercy with open contempt.

nuance.analogy: To spurn someone is like kicking a door shut in their face rather than simply saying no.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'spurnan,' meaning to kick or reject.
common_mistakes: Using 'spurn' in casual conversation where 'turn down' is more natural.
Confusing 'spurn' with 'spurt' or 'spin'; keep the final n clear.

spurn.etymology: From Middle English *spurnen*, *spornen*, from Old English *spurnan* (“to strike against, kick, spurn, reject; stumble”), from Proto-Germanic **spurnaną* (“to tread, kick, knock out”), from Proto-Indo-European **sperH-*.

senses.definition: A shaft in a multi-story building enclosing a stairway or staircase.

core.definition: The enclosed vertical shaft in a multi-story building that holds a staircase.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable ends in a clear l, so say well, not wall, and keep the r in stair strong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in crime or safety news it can sound eerie or unsafe.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stairwell for the enclosed stair space in apartments, offices and hospitals, often when talking about fire exits, safety or building access. In a house people usually say the stairs or staircase. In news stories about crime, stairwell carries an ominous tone because these spaces are often isolated.

distinctions.note: A staircase is the steps themselves; a stairwell is the enclosed shaft that holds them.
Stairway can be open or outdoors; stairwell is almost always enclosed and vertical.
An elevator shaft is for the lift; a stairwell is for people on foot.

examples.everyday: The neighbors heard someone talking in the stairwell late at night.
examples.professional: Please keep the stairwell doors closed, since they are fire-rated and part of our exit plan.
examples.analytical: The architect treated the stairwell as the building's spine, linking public floors with the routes of maintenance and escape.

nuance.analogy: A stairwell is like a building's spine: the steps are the vertebrae, and the walls protect what runs through them.
nuance.etymology: From stair plus well, meaning a vertical shaft or opening.
common_mistakes: Writing stair well as two words in formal or technical writing.
Using stairwell to mean the individual steps; the stairwell is the enclosed space around them.

senses.definition: A mass-produced plastic container of a standard size and shape containing a gelatinous bouillon.
senses.example: Each stock pot in the carton holds enough gelatinous bouillon for two cups of soup.

core.definition: A large pot for simmering bones, meat and vegetables for hours to make stock for soups and sauces.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on 'stock,' not on 'pot.' The vowel in 'stock' is the short 'ah' used in American 'cot,' and 'pot' has the same vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests home cooking, patience and a useful kitchen tool.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often write this as one word, 'stockpot,' especially on product labels and in recipes. In everyday talk they say 'stockpot' for a large pot used to make soup stock. It is not the same as a Dutch oven, which is for braising and baking, and the two are often confused by beginners.

distinctions.note: A Dutch oven is a heavy, lidded pot for braising and baking, while a stockpot is a tall pot for long simmering of liquids.
A saucepan is smaller and has a long handle for heating sauces, while a stockpot is large and tall for big batches.

examples.everyday: I always keep the stockpot on the back burner so I can make soup when the weather turns cold.
examples.professional: The commercial kitchen needs two new stockpots for the morning soup service.
examples.analytical: The stockpot concentrates flavor over hours, so the cook's patience matters as much as the ingredients.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow, patient kettle that turns scraps and bones into the base of many meals.
nuance.etymology: 'Stock' in the cooking sense from the idea of a store kept on hand, from Old English stocc, 'tree trunk'; 'pot' from Old English pott.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on 'pot' instead of 'stock.'
Confusing a stockpot with a Dutch oven or a saucepan.

senses.definition: To acquire or increase stock or inventory. [ with on]
senses.example: Q: What about fuel oil? A: We plan to stock up before November.

senses.definition: To swell up (usually refers to edema in a leg).
senses.example: Her ankle began to stock up after the long flight, so the doctor checked for a clot.

senses.definition: To extirpate; to dig up.
senses.example: The farmers worked all day to stock up the stumps that blocked the new field.

core.definition: To buy or gather a large supply of something so you have enough for later use.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on UP, the particle, not on stock. In fast speech the final k of stock links into the u of up, so it sounds like stah-KUP.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It suggests preparing ahead, sometimes for a storm or a holiday.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use stock up with on, as in stock up on water before the storm. Before a hurricane or a holiday weekend, people commonly say they are going to stock up. A natural reply to a friend announcing the plan is Good idea, I should too.

distinctions.note: Stockpile is more formal and often refers to large reserves kept for emergencies or government use, while stock up is everyday shopping language.
Buy in bulk focuses on purchasing large quantities at a lower price, while stock up focuses on building a supply for later.

examples.everyday: With the storm coming, I'm going to stock up on bottled water and canned soup this afternoon.
examples.professional: Procurement should stock up on printer toner before the end-of-quarter rush, so we don't run short.
examples.analytical: In a crisis, people stock up because they fear scarcity, and that fear can create the very shortages it anticipates.

nuance.analogy: Like filling a squirrel's cellar before winter, so there is food when the weather turns.
common_mistakes: Leaving out on before the object, as in stock up groceries instead of stock up on groceries.
Stressing stock in a way that makes the phrase sound like one long word.

conversation.text: I'm going to stock up on canned goods before the storm.
Toilet paper is on sale, so let's stock up.
We stocked up on school supplies during the summer sale.

senses.definition: One who throws stones.
A machine to remove the stones (pits) from fruit.
A habitual user of cannabis.
Someone or something that weighs a certain number of stones.

core.definition: Informally, a person who regularly uses marijuana.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the second syllable as a weak r-colored vowel, 'nur'. Do not make it two strong syllables.

nuance.connotation: Informal and often negative or teasing, depending on context. It can sound disrespectful.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'stoner' refers to a person who uses marijuana often, and is commonly used in a joking or dismissive way. It can also describe a stoner film or stoner culture. Americans rarely use it in serious or professional talk, so choose a neutral term like 'someone who uses marijuana regularly' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Pothead' is also informal and often more disparaging; 'stoner' is somewhat more casual and can describe a lifestyle or a film genre.
'User' is neutral and clinical, so it is better in professional or medical contexts than 'stoner'.

examples.everyday: My roommate is kind of a stoner, but he is a great cook.
examples.professional: Our HR policy applies to everyone, so a stoner comment at the company party would be treated as a conduct issue.
examples.analytical: The stoner genre in American film often mocks the cultural anxieties of its era.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone that sits still and never moves much, a stoner often seems slow and relaxed.
nuance.etymology: From 'stone' (verb, to pelt with stones) plus -er; the drug sense comes from 'stoned'.
common_mistakes: Using 'stoner' in a formal context; it sounds casual and judgmental.
Confusing it with the older sense 'one who throws stones'; that meaning is now rare.

stoner.etymology: From Middle English *stoner*, *stonere*, *stonare*, *staner*, equivalent to *stone* + *-er* or *-er*.

senses.definition: A sign by the side of a road or street, often at an intersection, instructing vehicle drivers to stop.

core.definition: A red octagonal sign at an intersection telling drivers they must come to a full stop before continuing.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SIGN, with a lighter stress on STOP. Keep the vowel in STOP short and open, and do not add a second syllable to SIGN, which is a single sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, functional term for a traffic sign.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase constantly when giving directions, such as 'Turn left at the stop sign.' Drivers also say 'run a stop sign' for ignoring one, which is a traffic violation. The sign itself is always red and octagonal across the United States.

distinctions.note: A stop sign requires a full stop, while a yield sign requires slowing down and giving way to other traffic only when necessary.
A stop sign is a fixed sign, while a traffic light is an electric signal that changes color.

collocations: come to a complete stop at a stop sign

examples.everyday: Turn right at the next stop sign and the store is on your left.
examples.professional: The city engineer said the new stop sign at Fifth and Main will reduce accidents at that corner.
examples.analytical: A stop sign is a rule encoded in a physical object, so its meaning depends on a shared cultural understanding among drivers.

nuance.analogy: A stop sign is like a full stop at the end of a sentence: the traffic must halt completely before it continues.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'stop' (from Old French estopper, to stop up) with 'sign' (from Latin signum, mark).
common_mistakes: Saying 'stop signal' for a sign, though 'stop sign' is the standard American term.
Pronouncing SIGN with two syllables, as in 'sy-gen'.

conversation.text: He rolled through the stop sign without stopping.
Come to a full stop at the stop sign, or you'll fail your driving test.
Turn left at the stop sign, and the house is the third one on the right.

senses.definition: A drinking straw.
A dried stalk of a cereal plant.
senses.example: The farmer bent down to pick a broken straw from the barn floor.

senses.definition: Such dried stalks considered collectively; this bulk matter may be a chief salable product, a by-product, fodder, bedding, or green manure, depending on region and on current market conditions.
senses.example: The truck hauled bales of straw to the dairy farm before the winter storms.

senses.definition: A pale, yellowish beige color, like that of a dried straw.
senses.example: straw:

senses.definition: Anything proverbially worthless; the least possible thing.
senses.example: to not care a straw

senses.definition: A straw owner.
senses.example: The real buyer used a straw to hide his name on the property deed.

senses.definition: Made of straw.
senses.example: straw hat

senses.definition: Of a pale, yellowish beige color, like that of a dried straw.
senses.example: The walls were painted a soft straw color that made the room feel warm.

senses.definition: Imaginary, but presented as real.
senses.example: A straw enemy built up in the media to seem like a real threat, which then collapses like a balloon.

senses.definition: To scatter or to spread loosely.
senses.example: Please straw the sawdust evenly across the floor before the guests arrive.

senses.definition: To lay straw around plants to protect them from frost.
senses.example: Gardeners straw the strawberry beds in late autumn to protect the roots from frost.

core.definition: A thin tube, usually of paper or plastic, used to sip a drink.

pronunciation.tip: The 'aw' vowel is a rounded open vowel, and the final 'w' is almost silent in the sense that it glides into the vowel. Many learners add an extra vowel sound after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'straw' every day at restaurants, especially with drinks. Restaurants often ask 'Do you want a straw?' Plastic straws have become a politically debated topic, and some people now ask for paper straws or no straw at all.

distinctions.note: A stirrer is used to mix a drink, while a straw is used to drink it.
Hay is cut and dried grass used as animal feed, while straw is the dried stalk of a cereal plant.

examples.everyday: Can I get a straw with my iced tea, please?
examples.professional: The cafeteria is switching to paper straws, so update the supply order before the event.
examples.analytical: The debate over plastic straws reveals how small consumer habits become symbols of larger environmental concerns.

nuance.analogy: Like a tiny tube that lets you pull the drink up from the bottom of the glass.
nuance.etymology: From Old English strēaw, 'straw, a stalk'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'straw' for a stirring stick, which is a different object.
Pronouncing it like 'stroh' with a long o, rather than the open 'aw' sound.

straw.etymology: From Middle English *straugh*, *strauȝ*, *straw*, *strawe*, *strea*, *streuw*, from Old English *strēaw*, *strēow*, from **strau*, from Proto-Germanic **strawą* (“that which is strewn, straw”), from Proto-Indo-European **strew-* (“to spread, strew”), from…

conversation.text: Can I get a straw for my drink?
Many restaurants now use paper straws.
When they lost our order, that was the last straw.

senses.definition: Full or packed (with some material or substance).
senses.example: Customs officers look closely through a stuffed suitcase.

senses.definition: Full after eating.
senses.example: Stuffed children sleep poorly.

senses.definition: Filled with a filling and seasoning.
senses.example: We're having stuffed turkey for dinner.

core.definition: Very full after eating a lot, often said in the phrase 'I'm stuffed' to mean you cannot eat anything more.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable ending in a hard 'ft' sound; the final 't' is a clear, crisp stop, not a flap. Avoid adding a vowel between 'f' and 't'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, 'I'm stuffed' is a common way to say you are too full to eat more, often after Thanksgiving dinner or a big meal. It is casual and friendly. In a restaurant, you might say 'I'm stuffed, but thanks' when the server offers dessert.

distinctions.note: Full is neutral and general, while stuffed suggests you have eaten so much that you feel uncomfortable.
Satisfied means your hunger is met without implying discomfort, while stuffed implies you may have eaten too much.

examples.everyday: Thanks, but I'm stuffed, so I'll skip dessert and just have coffee.
examples.professional: After the team lunch, most of us were stuffed, so the afternoon meeting ran quieter than usual.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'I'm stuffed' captures the bodily sensation of satiety that exceeds comfort, a state that everyday talk often reports with humor.

nuance.analogy: Being stuffed is like a suitcase packed so tightly that you cannot close it without pressing down hard.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of 'stuff,' from Old French 'estoffer,' to furnish or equip.
common_mistakes: Using 'stuffed' to mean simply 'full of interest' or 'satisfied' in a positive sense without the sense of excess.
Mispronouncing the final 'ft' as 'fed' or adding an extra vowel.

conversation.text: No dessert for me, thanks; I'm stuffed.
I ate too much bread, and now I'm stuffed.
I'll have the stuffed peppers with rice.
I'm stuffed; I couldn't eat another thing.
After Thanksgiving dinner, everyone was stuffed.
We had stuffed mushrooms as an appetizer.

senses.definition: To incapacitate; especially by inducing disorientation or unconsciousness.
senses.example: Bill tried to stun the snake by striking it on the head.

senses.definition: To shock or surprise.
senses.example: The celebrity was stunned to find herself confronted with unfounded allegations on the front page of a newspaper.

senses.definition: To hit the cue ball so that it slides without topspin or backspin (and with or without sidespin) and continues at a natural angle after contact with the object ball.
senses.example: To stun the cue ball, he struck it dead center, so it slid without any spin.

senses.definition: To enter a stunned state.
senses.example: The monsters stun when you jump on them.

senses.definition: The condition of being stunned.
That which stuns; a shock; a stupefying blow.
senses.example: The sudden layoff announcement was a real stun for the whole team.

senses.definition: A person who lacks intelligence.
senses.example: Honestly, that guy is a stun if he thinks the bridge is safe to cross.

senses.definition: The effect on the cue ball where the ball is hit without topspin, backspin or sidespin.
senses.example: Williams will need a lot of stun to avoid going in the middle pocket

senses.definition: A low-range setting for an energy weapon that will stun its target but not injure or kill it.
senses.example: The guard set his blaster to stun before the prisoner could reach the door.

core.definition: To knock someone dizzy or unconscious, or to shock someone so badly that they cannot react for a moment.

pronunciation.tip: Stun is one syllable with the short, relaxed vowel of cup, not the long oo of stoon. Say the final n clearly, and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in surprise contexts ('I was stunned by the news'); negative when it describes physical violence or a weapon that disables someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stunned constantly in everyday speech for surprise, good or bad: 'I was stunned when she quit.' The physical sense, as in a stun gun or a blow that stuns, is more serious and often comes up in news and crime reporting. In phrases, the past participle is more common than the base verb, so you will hear 'stunned silence' far more often than 'stun the room'.

distinctions.note: Shock often implies distress, offense or disbelief, while stun implies being momentarily unable to react at all.
Astonish is milder and more formal, and it usually describes admiration or amazement rather than a sudden blow to the senses.
Daze focuses on confusion or lack of focus, often physical; stun suggests a sharper, more sudden effect.

examples.everyday: I was stunned when my neighbor told me she had run a marathon at seventy.
examples.professional: The client was stunned by the price increase, so we need to walk them through the cost breakdown before Friday.
examples.analytical: Hume's argument is meant to stun the reader into doubting the causal inference that seems obvious to most people.

nuance.analogy: A stun is like a pause button pressed on your brain: everything keeps going around you, but you cannot move for a second.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stunian, meaning 'to make a loud noise or resound'; the sense of dazing developed later.
common_mistakes: Using stun with a long vowel, as in stoon; the vowel is short, like in fun.
Saying 'I was stun' instead of 'I was stunned'; the adjective form is the one used for people's feelings.

stun.etymology: Middle English *stonen*, *stone* (“to astonish, stun, numb”), probably either directly or indirectly from Anglo-Norman *estoner* (“to stun, astonish”), from Late Latin **stunō*, from **stunōn* (“to thunder, crash”) or perhaps from an unattested, from *tonō*.

senses.definition: To astonish or stun, especially as a result of some distressing action.
senses.example: The police's negligence and callousness continued to stupefy her.

senses.definition: To dull the senses or capacity to think thereby reducing responsiveness; to stun.
senses.example: a stupefying drug; a stupefacient

core.definition: To astonish or shock someone so greatly that they cannot think or react clearly; also to make someone dull and numb, as with boredom or a drug.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STOO, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. The final syllable is the diphthong 'fy' as in 'fly', so do not say 'stoo-PEE-fy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it can describe a pleasant shock but more often suggests numbness, dullness or distress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use stupefy in writing, speeches or formal conversation, and in the adjective 'stupefying' to describe boredom or heat. In everyday talk people usually say 'stunned', 'shocked', 'floored' or 'blown away'. Do not use it in casual conversation to mean 'make stupid', even though it sounds related to 'stupid'.

distinctions.note: Stun is more common and can be physical or sudden, while stupefy stresses a dulling or paralyzing effect on the mind.
Dumbfound is informal and means to leave someone speechless with surprise, whereas stupefy can also mean numbing or dulling.
Bewilder means to confuse someone, but stupefy suggests a stronger shock or dulling of thought.

examples.everyday: The heat in Phoenix in July is stupefying, so I just stay inside with the air conditioner on.
examples.professional: Honestly, the stupefying amount of approval forms is slowing the whole project, and nobody has time to read them.
examples.analytical: Marx argued that repetitive factory labor could stupefy the worker, dulling the very capacities that make reflection and resistance possible.

nuance.analogy: Like a bright light that blanks out a screen, stupefying shock washes out all thought for a moment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stupefacere, from stupere, 'be struck senseless', and facere, 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Saying stupefy to mean 'make someone look foolish' in casual speech; the word means shock or dulling.
Mispronouncing it as 'stoo-PID-fy' by blending it with 'stupid'.

stupefy.etymology: From Middle French *stupéfier*, from Latin *stupefaciō* (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from *stupeō* (“to be stunned, speechless”) (see English *stupid*, *stupor*) + *faciō* (“to do, make”).

senses.definition: Not meeting the minimum quality requirements.
senses.example: They built this with substandard parts. No wonder it collapsed.

senses.definition: (dated) Not conforming to the standard variety; nonstandard.
senses.example: Her teacher marked the sentence as substandard because it mixed dialects inconsistently.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Below the normal or required quality; not good enough for what it is supposed to do.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'STAN', the second syllable. The final '-ard' is reduced to a weak 'erd' with an r sound, so don't say it as a full 'ard'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies a clear failure to meet a required level.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use substandard for work, housing, goods and performance, as in 'substandard housing' or 'substandard work'. It is stronger than 'poor' because it implies a required standard was not met. The dated sense of 'nonstandard' for language is rarely used now; say 'nonstandard English' instead.

distinctions.note: Poor is general and can describe anything of low quality, while substandard implies that a specific accepted standard was not met.
Inferior compares one thing to another as lower in quality, while substandard says something falls below an acceptable level.

examples.everyday: The service at that restaurant was substandard, and our food came out cold twice.
examples.professional: The vendor delivered substandard code, so QA sent it back before the release.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that substandard public schools often reflect funding gaps rather than the effort of their teachers.

nuance.analogy: Like a shirt with a loose seam: it can still be worn, but it does not meet the tailor's standard.
nuance.etymology: From sub- 'below' and standard.
common_mistakes: Calling a person substandard in casual talk, which sounds harsh; say 'underperforming' instead.
Confusing it with 'nonstandard', which means not the usual form, while substandard means below acceptable quality.

senses.definition: The state of being substantial; substantialness.
The extent to which something is substantial.
senses.example: The judge questioned the substantiality of the evidence before allowing the trial to proceed.

core.definition: The quality of being large, solid or real in amount, weight or importance.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'AL', the fourth syllable, with a lighter stress on 'STAN'. Non-natives often shift the stress to 'stan' or pronounce 'shee' as 'shay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a quality without praising or criticizing it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use substantiality. It appears in philosophy, law and formal writing when discussing how real or weighty something is. In speech, say 'how substantial it is' or 'how much it matters' instead.

distinctions.note: Substance is the matter or content itself, while substantiality is the quality of being substantial, large or real.
Substantiation means providing evidence that proves something, while substantiality means the quality of being real or considerable.

collocations: question the substantiality of the claim

examples.everyday: The chili was so thick and hearty that it had real substantiality, and nobody wanted dessert.
examples.professional: We need to judge the substantiality of the risk before the board meets, not just its likelihood.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique presses on the substantiality of the self, asking whether any solid substratum lies beneath our perceptions.

nuance.analogy: Like the weight of a stone compared with a balloon: you can feel the difference in your hands.
nuance.etymology: From substantial, from Latin substantialis, from substantia; the -ity suffix forms a noun of quality.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'substance' or 'substantiation': substance is the matter itself, and substantiation is proof.
Pronouncing the final '-ity' as 'ee-tee'; it is 'ih-tee' with a weak final vowel.

senses.definition: To make suburban; to convert or adapt to a suburb.

core.definition: To change an area so that it becomes suburban, usually by building housing, roads, and shopping outside a city.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on BUR, and a weaker secondary stress falls on the final syllable, NIZE. The first and second vowels are reduced to schwas, so the word moves smoothly from 'suh' to 'buh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in planning and economics. It can be negative when people feel that farmland or a community is losing its character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use suburbanize mainly in urban planning, real estate, news about growth, and academic writing. In everyday talk they usually say that an area is 'turning into suburbs' or 'getting developed.' The word sounds technical in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Gentrify means that a poor urban neighborhood becomes wealthier and more middle-class, while suburbanize means that an area on the edge becomes suburban.
Urbanize means to make an area more like a city, the opposite process of suburbanize.

examples.everyday: My uncle is upset that developers are suburbanizing the farm fields where he grew up.
